q: A company is migrating its self-managed Kafka cluster to AWS. It needs brokers spread across AZs with automatic broker replacement and wants to avoid running ZooKeeper. Which service provides managed Kafka with these properties?
options: Amazon SQS
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon MSK with multi-AZ broker deployment — managed Kafka with automatic broker recovery, and KRaft mode removes the ZooKeeper dependency
Amazon SNS
explain: MSK is the managed Apache Kafka service: brokers span AZs, failed brokers are replaced automatically, and KRaft mode eliminates ZooKeeper. SQS is a message queue without Kafka semantics, Kinesis is a different streaming model, and SNS is pub/sub fan-out.

q: A Redshift cluster slows to a crawl every Monday morning when hundreds of analysts run reports simultaneously, but it sits mostly idle the rest of the week. Which feature automatically adds transient query capacity during these bursts?
options: Permanently resizing to a larger node type
Concurrency scaling — automatically provisions additional clusters to absorb burst query load
Adding more persistent storage
Taking more frequent snapshots
explain: Concurrency scaling adds transient clusters automatically when the main cluster's queues fill, then removes them — paying only for burst seconds. A permanently larger node type wastes money all week, storage doesn't add query throughput, and snapshots are for recovery.

q: A gaming leaderboard on ElastiCache for Redis is hitting the memory and throughput limits of a single primary node. The workload shards cleanly by player ID. Which configuration scales Redis horizontally?
options: Enable Redis cluster mode with data sharded across multiple shards
Add read replicas to the single shard
Switch the workload to Memcached
Vertically scale to the largest available node type
explain: Cluster mode shards data across shards, scaling both memory and throughput horizontally for partitionable workloads. Read replicas add read capacity but not memory or write throughput, switching engines doesn't change the single-node limit, and vertical scaling hits a ceiling.

q: A global video platform's origin is overwhelmed by cache misses: many CloudFront edge locations each fetch the same unpopular content from the origin independently. Which feature adds an intermediate caching layer to collapse these origin requests?
options: Adding more origin servers
Setting longer TTLs on every object
CloudFront Origin Shield — an additional caching layer in the regional edge cache that consolidates origin fetches
Using signed URLs for all content
explain: Origin Shield designates one regional edge cache per Region as the single fetcher from the origin, so misses from many edge locations collapse into one origin request. More origins add cost without collapsing fetches, TTLs can't be raised on dynamic content, and signed URLs control access rather than origin load.

q: A public API backed by Lambda is abused by a few clients sending thousands of requests per second, degrading service for everyone else. Which API Gateway features protect the backend from abusive clients?
options: Enabling CORS on the API
Distributing API keys without any limits
Increasing the Lambda function's memory
Usage plans with API keys and per-client throttling quotas
explain: Usage plans bind API keys to throttle and quota limits, so abusive clients are rate-limited without affecting others. CORS enables cross-origin browser access, keys without limits identify but don't restrain clients, and Lambda memory doesn't cap request rates.

q: An application downloads 20 GB files from S3, but users typically need only the first few megabytes containing the file headers. Which technique minimizes data transfer?
options: Enabling S3 Transfer Acceleration
Byte-range fetches (Range GET requests) to download only the needed portions of each object
Using S3 multipart upload
Enabling cross-region replication
explain: Range GET requests retrieve only specified byte ranges, so the application transfers megabytes instead of gigabytes. Transfer Acceleration speeds the transfer without shrinking it, multipart upload is for uploads, and replication copies whole objects.

q: A DynamoDB table serves steady, predictable traffic with gradual month-over-month growth. The team wants automatic capacity adjustments without paying per-request premiums. Which capacity configuration is BEST?
options: Provisioned mode with auto scaling — adjusts RCU/WCU toward target utilization as traffic grows
On-demand mode
Fixed provisioned capacity set once a year
Adding DAX in front of the table
explain: Provisioned auto scaling tracks steady predictable growth at provisioned-mode pricing, which is cheaper than on-demand for sustained traffic. On-demand charges a premium per request that adds up on steady workloads, fixed capacity throttles as traffic grows, and DAX is a cache rather than a capacity strategy.

q: Athena queries against 10 TB of S3 log data are slow and expensive because every query scans the entire dataset. The data includes a date field and queries almost always filter by date. Which change reduces the scanned data the MOST?
options: Using a larger Athena workgroup
Enabling S3 Transfer Acceleration
Partitioning the data by date so queries scan only the relevant prefixes
Moving the data to S3 Standard-IA
explain: Partitioning by date lets Athena prune entire prefixes, so a one-day query scans gigabytes instead of terabytes — cutting both latency and cost. Workgroup size doesn't reduce scanned bytes, Transfer Acceleration affects uploads, and storage class doesn't change how much Athena scans.

q: A mission-critical database workload needs 100,000 sustained IOPS from a single EBS volume with sub-millisecond latency and the highest durability. Which volume type meets this requirement?
options: gp3, which maxes out at 16,000 provisioned IOPS
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
io1, which maxes out at 64,000 IOPS
io2 Block Express, which supports up to 256,000 IOPS per volume with sub-millisecond latency
explain: io2 Block Express is purpose-built for extreme IOPS (up to 256,000 per volume) with 99.999% durability. gp3 caps at 16,000 IOPS, io1 caps at 64,000, and HDD types are throughput-oriented — none reach 100,000 IOPS on one volume.

q: A company runs 20 microservices as ECS tasks and wants a single ALB to route api.example.com to one service and admin.example.com to another, without paying for a load balancer per service. Which ALB feature enables this?
options: Deploying one ALB per microservice
Host-based routing rules that forward by the Host header
Replacing the ALB with a Network Load Balancer
Enabling sticky sessions
explain: Host-based (and path-based) listener rules let one ALB route to many target groups by hostname, consolidating microservices behind a single load balancer. One ALB per service multiplies cost, an NLB can't route on HTTP hostnames, and sticky sessions pin users to targets rather than routing by host.

q: A Java-based Lambda function suffers 5-second cold starts caused by JVM initialization, hurting user experience after idle periods. Which feature restores a pre-initialized execution environment snapshot to cut these cold starts?
options: Lambda SnapStart — restores a pre-initialized snapshot of the execution environment
Increasing the function memory to the maximum
Packaging dependencies in a larger deployment package
Configuring Lambda destinations
explain: SnapStart takes a snapshot of the initialized execution environment (including the warmed JVM) and restores it on cold start, slashing Java initialization time. More memory speeds execution but not JVM init proportionally, larger packages slow cold starts, and destinations handle async results.

q: A video transcoding fleet is heavily CPU-bound while memory sits idle at 15% utilization. The team is overpaying for unused RAM on general-purpose instances. Which EC2 instance family gives the best price-performance for this workload?
options: Memory-optimized (R family)
Storage-optimized (I family)
Compute-optimized (C family) with a high vCPU-to-memory ratio
General purpose (M family)
explain: Compute-optimized instances pack more vCPU per dollar and per GB of RAM, matching CPU-bound transcoding. Memory-optimized instances waste spend on unneeded RAM, storage-optimized targets local NVMe I/O, and general purpose keeps the same imbalance.

q: An Aurora cluster has spiky, unpredictable I/O, and the pay-per-I/O charges are dominating the database bill. The workload is I/O-intensive enough that a predictable pricing model would be cheaper. Which configuration addresses this?
options: Increasing the DB instance size
Adding more Aurora Replicas
Migrating to Aurora Serverless v1
Aurora I/O-Optimized — predictable pricing designed for I/O-intensive workloads
explain: I/O-Optimized replaces per-million-I/O charges with a predictable uplift, which wins for consistently I/O-heavy clusters. Bigger instances don't change the I/O billing model, replicas add read capacity rather than cheaper I/O, and Serverless v1 has its own different pricing.

q: A data warehouse holds 2 TB of hot data queried constantly and 50 TB of historical data queried occasionally. The team wants to scale compute and storage independently instead of buying large nodes for the full 52 TB. Which Redshift architecture fits?
options: Dense Compute (DC2) nodes with local SSDs
RA3 nodes with managed storage — compute scales separately from virtually unlimited managed storage
A single-node cluster
Keeping all 52 TB on provisioned local SSDs
explain: RA3 with managed storage decouples compute from storage, so the team sizes nodes for the hot 2 TB workload while 50 TB lives cheaply in managed storage. DC2 ties storage to node-local SSDs, single-node can't hold the data, and provisioning SSDs for all 52 TB massively overpays.

q: Applications in private subnets call DynamoDB and Amazon SQS through a NAT gateway, adding latency and data processing charges to every request. Which change provides private, low-latency access to these services?
options: VPC endpoints — a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB and interface endpoints for SQS keep traffic on the private AWS network
Moving the applications to public subnets
Deploying a larger NAT gateway
Adding internet gateway routes to the private subnets
explain: VPC endpoints route service traffic privately without NAT hops, cutting both latency and data processing charges. Public subnets expose the applications, a bigger NAT gateway still charges per GB, and internet gateway routes in private subnets defeat their purpose.

q: Three consumer applications read from the same Kinesis data stream, and each consumer is throttled because they share the 2 MB/s per-shard read limit. The team wants each consumer to have dedicated read throughput without resharding. Which feature provides this?
options: Increasing the shard count
Reducing the retention period
Enhanced fan-out — each registered consumer gets dedicated 2 MB/s per-shard throughput
Switching to SQS standard queues
explain: Enhanced fan-out pushes records to each registered consumer over HTTP/2 with its own dedicated throughput, eliminating the shared 2 MB/s contention. More shards increase total throughput but every consumer still shares it, retention doesn't affect read limits, and SQS is a different messaging model.

q: A DynamoDB table keyed by order ID must also support efficient queries by customer ID and order date. Full table scans are too slow and expensive. Which feature enables this alternate access pattern?
options: Adding DAX in front of the table
Enabling DynamoDB Streams
Running scans with filter expressions
Creating a global secondary index (GSI) on customer ID and order date
explain: A GSI provides an alternate key structure with its own provisioned throughput, enabling efficient keyed queries by customer and date. DAX caches but doesn't add query patterns, Streams capture changes for processing, and filtered scans still read the whole table.

q: An application retrieves large JSON documents from S3 but must mask PII fields with custom business logic before the data reaches callers. Downloading full objects and masking in the application wastes bandwidth. Which feature transforms objects during retrieval?
options: S3 Select with SQL filtering
S3 Object Lambda — a Lambda function transforms (e.g., redacts PII from) objects as they are retrieved
CloudFront Functions
Replicating the bucket to more Regions
explain: Object Lambda invokes custom code on GET requests, so PII masking happens server-side and callers receive only redacted data. S3 Select filters with SQL but can't run custom masking logic, CloudFront Functions run at edge locations rather than on S3 retrieval, and replication doesn't transform content.

q: A workflow orchestrates 5 million short-lived, event-driven executions per day. Standard Step Functions workflows are becoming expensive at this volume. Which workflow type is optimized for high-volume, short-duration executions?
options: Express Workflows — optimized for high event rates and short durations with lower per-execution cost
Standard Workflows
Amazon SWF
Replacing orchestration with SQS alone
explain: Express Workflows are priced and engineered for millions of brief executions (up to 5 minutes), costing far less than Standard at this volume. Standard suits long-running durable workflows, SWF is the legacy predecessor, and SQS alone loses the orchestration state machine.

q: An ECS Fargate service behind an ALB sees CPU spikes during marketing campaigns, and manual task-count changes are always late. Which feature automatically adjusts the task count based on demand signals like ALB request count or CPU?
options: Manually updating the desired task count before each campaign
Switching the service to Fargate Spot
ECS Service Auto Scaling with target tracking policies
Increasing the CPU and memory of each task
explain: Service Auto Scaling with target tracking adds and removes tasks automatically based on metrics like ALB RequestCountPerTarget or CPU utilization. Manual changes lag demand, Fargate Spot changes pricing rather than scaling, and bigger tasks don't scale horizontally.

q: An RDS database suffers intermittent slow queries. The team wants query-level performance analysis — which queries are slow and why — with minimal overhead and no agents to manage. Which feature provides this?
options: AWS CloudTrail
Manually exporting the slow query log to CloudWatch
Enabling Multi-AZ deployment
RDS Performance Insights — visualizes DB load by wait event and top SQL with lightweight instrumentation
explain: Performance Insights samples database activity with minimal overhead and breaks down load by SQL statement and wait events, pinpointing the slow queries. CloudTrail audits API calls rather than query performance, manual log exports are toil-heavy, and Multi-AZ addresses failover.

q: A Redis cache serves 100,000 reads per second and the single primary node is saturated, while writes remain light. Which ElastiCache scaling approach adds read capacity with the LEAST disruption?
options: Resharding a cluster-mode deployment
Adding Redis read replicas to scale read throughput
Migrating the workload to Memcached
Disabling Redis persistence
explain: Read replicas offload read traffic from the primary with no resharding and minimal disruption — ideal for read-heavy, write-light workloads. Resharding is heavier and meant for memory/write scaling, switching engines is a rewrite, and disabling persistence doesn't add throughput.

q: An application needs 8,000 sustained IOPS on a 500 GB volume. With gp2, the team would have to over-provision to nearly 3 TB just to get the IOPS. Which volume type delivers 8,000 IOPS on a 500 GB volume at lower cost?
options: gp3 — 3,000 baseline IOPS included, with IOPS provisionable up to 16,000 independently of volume size
io2 Block Express
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
Cold HDD (sc1)
explain: gp3 decouples IOPS from capacity, so 8,000 IOPS on 500 GB costs far less than a 3 TB gp2 volume or premium io2. io2 is overkill and pricier for this IOPS level, and HDD types can't deliver provisioned IOPS.

q: A FIFO queue must sustain 3,000 messages per second, but throughput caps at 300 messages per second even with batching. What enables higher FIFO throughput?
options: Switching to a standard queue
Adding more consumers
Enabling high throughput mode for FIFO queues
Increasing the visibility timeout
explain: High throughput mode for FIFO raises the limit to 3,000 messages per second with batching by relaxing ordering scope across message groups. A standard queue abandons ordering guarantees, more consumers don't raise the per-queue limit, and visibility timeout affects redelivery timing.

q: An EMR Spark cluster is manually sized for peak load and sits idle 70% of the day, wasting spend. Which EMR feature automatically resizes the cluster based on the actual workload?
options: Provisioning larger core nodes
Running everything on Spot Instances
Increasing step concurrency
EMR managed scaling — automatically adds and removes nodes based on workload demands
explain: Managed scaling monitors YARN metrics and resizes the cluster automatically, matching capacity to demand. Larger nodes worsen idle waste, Spot changes pricing rather than sizing, and step concurrency parallelizes steps without resizing the cluster.

q: A CloudFront distribution caches everything for 24 hours, including personalized API responses, so users receive stale data. Which configuration fixes caching behavior per content type?
options: Disabling CloudFront entirely
Cache policies with appropriate TTLs and cache keys per cache behavior — long TTLs for static assets, short or no caching for dynamic API paths
Requiring signed URLs for all requests
Enabling Origin Shield
explain: Per-behavior cache policies set the right TTL and cache key for each content type, so static assets cache long while dynamic responses stay fresh. Disabling CloudFront loses global performance, signed URLs control access rather than freshness, and Origin Shield reduces origin load without fixing stale caching.

q: An IAM user has two policies attached: one allows s3:* on a bucket, and another explicitly denies s3:DeleteObject on that bucket. The user attempts to delete an object. What happens?
options: The delete is denied — an explicit deny always overrides any allow
The delete is allowed because the allow policy is more specific
The delete is allowed because the allow policy was attached first
The delete proceeds but requires MFA
explain: In IAM policy evaluation, an explicit deny wins over any allow regardless of specificity or attachment order. The 'more specific' and 'attached first' ideas are common misconceptions — neither affects evaluation — and MFA isn't triggered by policy conflicts.

q: Developers need permission to create their own IAM roles for new services, but the security team must guarantee that no developer-created role can ever receive administrator-level permissions. Which mechanism caps the maximum permissions any of these roles can hold?
options: Service Control Policies on the accounts
Resource-based policies on each service
IAM permissions boundaries — set the maximum permissions an identity can receive regardless of its attached policies
Rotating access keys frequently
explain: A permissions boundary defines the maximum effective permissions for a user or role, so even a broad attached policy can't exceed it. SCPs restrict at the account level rather than per-role delegation, resource policies control who accesses a resource rather than capping a role, and key rotation doesn't limit permissions.

q: A company with 500 employees needs centralized single sign-on to AWS accounts and business applications, with enforced MFA and automated user provisioning and deprovisioning. Which is the AWS-recommended approach?
options: Creating IAM users in every account
Sharing a small set of IAM users per team
Using long-term access keys stored in a vault
IAM Identity Center — centralized SSO with MFA enforcement and SCIM provisioning
explain: IAM Identity Center provides one identity source with SSO across accounts and apps, centralized MFA enforcement, and automated provisioning. Per-account IAM users multiply credential sprawl, shared users destroy auditability, and long-term keys are the weakest credential type.

q: Account A needs read access to an S3 bucket in Account B. The bucket policy in Account B grants access to a role in Account A. The access still fails. What else is required?
options: Nothing — the bucket policy alone is sufficient
The role's identity-based policy in Account A must also allow the S3 actions (cross-account access requires both policies to permit)
Making the bucket publicly readable
Establishing VPC peering between the accounts
explain: Cross-account access requires permission on both sides: the resource policy in Account B and the identity policy in Account A. A bucket policy alone isn't enough when the principal is in another account, public access is never the answer, and VPC peering is irrelevant to S3 policy evaluation.

q: An application in Account A must decrypt data using a KMS key in Account B. The key policy in Account B grants the application's role kms:Decrypt. The decryption still fails with AccessDenied. What is missing?
options: The IAM policy on the role in Account A must also allow kms:Decrypt on the key — KMS evaluates both the key policy and the identity policy for cross-account use
Nothing — the key policy alone is sufficient
Enabling automatic key rotation
Creating a VPC endpoint for KMS
explain: Unlike some AWS services, KMS requires both the key policy and the caller's identity policy to allow the action for cross-account calls. The key policy alone doesn't suffice, rotation is about key lifecycle rather than authorization, and a VPC endpoint affects network path rather than permissions.

q: A bank must manage its own encryption keys in dedicated, single-tenant hardware validated to FIPS 140-2 Level 3, with a guarantee that AWS operators have no access to the keys. Which service meets this requirement?
options: AWS KMS with AWS-managed keys
SSE-S3 with Amazon S3-managed keys
AWS CloudHSM — dedicated single-tenant HSMs under exclusive customer control
AWS Certificate Manager
explain: CloudHSM provides single-tenant hardware security modules where the customer exclusively controls the keys, meeting strict regulatory demands. KMS is multi-tenant (keys are logically isolated but hardware is shared), SSE-S3 uses AWS-managed keys, and ACM manages TLS certificates rather than general encryption keys.

q: A company needs stateful Layer 3 through Layer 7 inspection, intrusion prevention, and domain-based egress filtering for traffic leaving its VPC. Security groups and NACLs cannot provide this. Which service offers managed network firewall capabilities?
options: AWS WAF
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Shield Advanced
AWS Network Firewall — managed stateful inspection, IPS rules, and URL/domain filtering for VPC traffic
explain: Network Firewall is the managed VPC firewall with stateful rule groups, Suricata-compatible IPS signatures, and domain-list egress filtering. WAF inspects Layer 7 web requests at ALB/CloudFront rather than VPC traffic, GuardDuty is detective threat detection, and Shield mitigates DDoS.

q: A company with 40 AWS accounts needs consistent WAF rules on every ALB and automatic enforcement when new resources are created. Which service centrally manages security policies across the organization?
options: AWS Config
AWS Firewall Manager — centrally deploys and maintains WAF, Shield, and security group policies across accounts
Amazon Inspector
AWS CloudTrail
explain: Firewall Manager uses AWS Organizations to push baseline WAF rules, Shield protections, and security group policies to all accounts and auto-remediates drift on new resources. Config evaluates compliance but doesn't deploy WAF rules, Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, and CloudTrail audits API activity.

q: A security team needs a single aggregated view of findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie across all accounts and Regions, normalized with standard severity levels. Which service provides this central security dashboard?
options: AWS Security Hub — aggregates and normalizes findings from security services into one view
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards
Amazon Detective
AWS Artifact
explain: Security Hub collects findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and others into a single normalized, cross-account view with automated compliance checks. CloudWatch dashboards show metrics rather than security findings, Detective investigates root causes of specific findings, and Artifact hosts compliance reports.

q: A company wants automated vulnerability scanning of container images pushed to ECR and continuous CVE assessment of EC2 instances, without deploying agents where possible. Which service provides this?
options: Amazon GuardDuty
AWS WAF
Amazon Inspector — scans ECR images on push and EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities and network exposure
Amazon Macie
explain: Inspector is the vulnerability management service: it scans ECR images on push and assesses EC2 instances for CVEs and unintended network paths, agentless for ECR. GuardDuty detects threats from logs rather than scanning for CVEs, WAF filters web traffic, and Macie finds sensitive data in S3.

q: A mobile app authenticates users through the company's corporate SAML identity provider and needs to give the app temporary AWS credentials for direct S3 access. Which Cognito component brokers federated identities into temporary AWS credentials?
options: Cognito user pools
IAM users for each app customer
AWS Certificate Manager
Cognito identity pools (federated identities) — exchange IdP tokens for temporary AWS credentials
explain: Identity pools federate external identity providers (SAML, social, OIDC) and vend temporary AWS credentials scoped by IAM roles. User pools handle sign-up/sign-in but don't issue AWS credentials, IAM users per customer is an anti-pattern, and ACM manages certificates.

q: A company needs TLS certificates for internal services with private DNS names. Public CAs won't issue them, and the team wants automated issuance and renewal inside the organization. Which service provides a managed private certificate authority?
options: ACM public certificates
ACM Private CA — a managed private CA for internal certificates with automated issuance and renewal
Manually generated self-signed certificates
AWS KMS
explain: ACM Private CA runs a managed private CA hierarchy so internal services get trusted certificates with automated lifecycle. ACM public certificates can't cover non-public names, manual self-signed certificates create renewal toil and trust issues, and KMS manages encryption keys rather than certificates.

q: Applications in multiple VPCs need to resolve internal service names like db.internal without sending DNS queries over the internet. Which Route 53 feature provides private DNS resolution?
options: Private hosted zones associated with the VPCs
A public hosted zone
Geolocation routing policies
Resolver endpoints alone
explain: Private hosted zones answer DNS queries only from associated VPCs, keeping internal names off the public internet. A public hosted zone exposes names globally, geolocation is a routing policy rather than a zone type, and Resolver endpoints forward queries rather than authoritatively serving private names.

q: Remote employees need secure access to private resources in a VPC from their laptops, without deploying site-to-site hardware at each home office. Which service provides managed client-based VPN access?
options: AWS Direct Connect
Site-to-Site VPN
AWS Client VPN — managed OpenVPN-based access for individual devices
A NAT gateway
explain: Client VPN is purpose-built for remote users connecting from laptops and phones, with IAM and Active Directory authentication options. Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN connect networks rather than roaming clients, and a NAT gateway provides outbound internet access, not inbound VPN.

q: A company wants zero-trust access to internal web applications: every request evaluated against user identity and device posture, with no VPN client to install or manage. Which service provides this?
options: AWS Client VPN
Security groups on the application load balancer
AWS Direct Connect
AWS Verified Access — policy-based zero-trust application access without a VPN
explain: Verified Access evaluates identity and device trust per request via access policies, granting application access without VPN tunnels. Client VPN still requires a client and grants network-level access, security groups are static network rules, and Direct Connect is private network connectivity.

q: A team stores 500 non-secret configuration values (feature flags, endpoints, timeouts) and wants hierarchical organization, versioning, and no per-item monthly cost. Which is the MOST cost-effective choice?
options: AWS Secrets Manager for every value
SSM Parameter Store (Standard tier) — hierarchical parameters with versioning at no per-parameter charge
Hardcoding the values in application code
A DynamoDB table with manual versioning
explain: Parameter Store Standard tier is free and purpose-built for hierarchical configuration with versioning. Secrets Manager charges per secret per month — wasteful for non-secrets — hardcoding prevents updates without redeploys, and DynamoDB adds unnecessary operational overhead for simple config.

q: A company suspects compromised credentials are being used to list and exfiltrate data from S3 buckets. Which GuardDuty protection plan specifically monitors S3 data-plane API activity for malicious patterns?
options: GuardDuty S3 Protection — analyzes CloudTrail S3 data events for threats like anomalous access
AWS WAF
Amazon Macie
Amazon Inspector
explain: S3 Protection is the GuardDuty plan that profiles S3 data-event activity to detect exfiltration and anomalous access. WAF filters web requests, Macie discovers sensitive data rather than detecting active threats, and Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities.

q: A company must continuously verify that all S3 buckets have versioning enabled and all EBS volumes are encrypted, across 30 accounts, with a centralized compliance dashboard. Which solution provides this?
options: AWS CloudTrail alone
AWS Trusted Advisor checks alone
AWS Config rules packaged in conformance packs, with aggregated compliance data across accounts
Amazon GuardDuty
explain: Config rules continuously evaluate resource configuration against desired state, conformance packs bundle related rules, and aggregators centralize results across accounts. CloudTrail records API calls rather than evaluating configuration, Trusted Advisor checks are point-in-time and less customizable, and GuardDuty detects threats rather than configuration compliance.

q: A DevOps team wants to detect unusual API activity — for example, a sudden spike in EC2 terminations or IAM policy changes — without writing custom log analysis. Which CloudTrail feature uses machine learning to surface anomalous activity?
options: Log file integrity validation
S3 server access logging
VPC Flow Logs
CloudTrail Insights — ML models detect unusual management-event activity and raise findings
explain: Insights builds baselines of normal API activity and flags statistically unusual bursts, such as mass terminations. Log file validation detects tampering rather than anomalies, S3 access logs record object access, and Flow Logs capture network traffic — none apply ML to API behavior.

q: A security audit must identify IAM users with passwords older than 90 days and access keys that have never been rotated. Which report provides credential age and rotation status for every IAM user?
options: The AWS Cost and Usage Report
The IAM credential report — lists password age, key age, and MFA status per user
CloudTrail event history
Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
explain: The credential report is purpose-built for audits, showing password last-changed, access key age and last use, and MFA status for all IAM users. The CUR tracks spend, CloudTrail event history covers only recent API calls rather than credential metadata, and Trusted Advisor cost checks optimize billing.

q: Three teams share one S3 bucket holding a common dataset, but each team must access different prefixes with different permissions. Maintaining one giant bucket policy has become error-prone. Which feature simplifies per-team access management?
options: S3 Access Points — named network endpoints with their own access policies per team or application
Creating three separate buckets with replication between them
Making the bucket public and filtering in the application
Creating IAM users named after each object prefix
explain: Access Points let each team get its own hostname and policy scoped to its prefixes, decomposing one complex bucket policy into manageable pieces. Separate buckets with replication multiply storage and sync complexity, public buckets are never acceptable, and IAM users can't be scoped per prefix cleanly.

q: A compliance audit requires TLS 1.2 or higher on all load balancers and forbids deprecated cipher suites. Where is the TLS version and cipher selection enforced on an Application Load Balancer?
options: In the security group attached to the ALB
In the target group settings
In the ALB listener's security policy (e.g., ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06)
In the subnet network ACL
explain: The listener security policy defines the TLS protocol versions and ciphers the ALB negotiates. Security groups filter ports rather than TLS versions, target groups handle backend routing and health checks, and NACLs are stateless subnet packet filters.

q: A login API is under credential-stuffing attack from a botnet rotating through thousands of IP addresses, each staying just under naive per-IP limits. Which WAF rule type automatically blocks IPs that exceed a request threshold within a time window?
options: AWS managed SQLi rule group
Geo match rules
String match rules on the User-Agent header
Rate-based rules — track request rates per IP and block offenders automatically
explain: Rate-based rules count requests per IP over a sliding window and block IPs exceeding the threshold, which is the direct counter to credential stuffing. SQLi rules target injection payloads, geo match blocks countries rather than abusive rates, and string matching on headers is easily evaded by rotating user agents.

q: A streaming company must block access to licensed content from specific countries while serving it everywhere else. Which CloudFront feature enforces country-level blocking?
options: CloudFront signed URLs
CloudFront geo restriction (geoblocking) — allowlist or blocklist countries at the edge
AWS WAF SQLi managed rules
Origin Access Control
explain: Geo restriction blocks or allows viewers by country at CloudFront edge locations before content is served. Signed URLs control who can access content rather than where, WAF SQLi rules target injection attacks, and OAC restricts S3 access to CloudFront rather than filtering by viewer country.

q: A company stores API keys for a third-party SaaS product in Secrets Manager and needs automatic rotation. The SaaS product is not an RDS database, so no built-in rotation template applies. How is automatic rotation achieved?
options: Write a custom Lambda rotation function that Secrets Manager invokes on schedule to rotate the SaaS API key
Secrets Manager automatically rotates any secret type with no configuration
Rotate the keys manually in the console each month
Move the keys to Parameter Store, which rotates everything automatically
explain: Secrets Manager supports custom Lambda rotation functions for non-RDS credentials, invoked on the configured schedule. There is no automatic rotation without a rotation function, manual rotation is toil-prone and often skipped, and Parameter Store doesn't rotate secrets natively.

q: A company will run steady EC2 workloads for 3 years but expects to change instance families as new generations are released. Which commitment gives a deep discount while allowing instance family changes?
options: Standard Reserved Instances
On-Demand Instances
Convertible Reserved Instances — can be exchanged for different instance families during the term
Spot Instances
explain: Convertible RIs trade some discount depth for flexibility, allowing exchanges across instance families as needs evolve. Standard RIs lock the instance family, On-Demand has no commitment discount, and Spot offers no price certainty for steady workloads.

q: A Spot fleet keeps suffering mass interruptions during peak hours because every instance is the same type in a single AZ — one capacity crunch wipes out the whole fleet. Which best practice MOST improves Spot availability?
options: Diversify across multiple instance types, sizes, and AZs with the capacity-optimized allocation strategy
Use larger instances of the same type
Consolidate into a single AZ for simplicity
Replace Spot with On-Demand entirely
explain: Diversification spreads interruption risk across many independent capacity pools, and the capacity-optimized strategy picks pools with the most spare capacity. Larger same-type instances share the same pool risk, single-AZ concentrates it, and abandoning Spot forfeits the discount instead of fixing the design.

q: A data lake stores 500 million tiny 2 KB objects in S3 Standard with heavy PUT/GET churn. The storage itself is cheap, yet the monthly bill is enormous. What is the likely dominant cost driver?
options: Data transfer out to the internet
KMS key usage charges
Cross-region replication
Per-request charges — hundreds of millions of PUT, GET, and LIST requests dwarf the storage cost of tiny objects
explain: S3 request pricing is per-request regardless of object size, so half a billion tiny objects with churn makes API charges dominate. Data transfer only bills on egress, KMS charges are comparatively small, and replication wasn't mentioned as enabled.

q: Two chatty application tiers transfer 50 TB per month between Availability Zones, incurring cross-AZ data transfer charges. The tiers are tightly coupled and always deploy together. Which architectural change eliminates these charges?
options: Using larger EC2 instances
Co-locating the tightly coupled tiers in the same AZ — data transfer within an AZ is free
Spreading the tiers across even more AZs
Routing the traffic through a NAT gateway
explain: Same-AZ data transfer incurs no charge, so co-locating chatty tiers removes the 50 TB/month fee. Larger instances don't change transfer pricing, more AZs multiply cross-AZ traffic, and NAT gateways add their own data processing charges. The tradeoff to note: this reduces AZ-level resilience, so it suits tiers that already deploy as a unit.

q: A team enabled detailed (1-minute) monitoring on every instance and created thousands of custom metrics and alarms; the CloudWatch bill has spiked. Which change reduces cost while keeping essential visibility?
options: Revert non-critical resources to basic monitoring and prune unused custom metrics and alarms
Build more CloudWatch dashboards
Delete all alarms
Increase metric retention to 15 months
explain: Detailed monitoring, custom metrics, and alarms are each billed — trimming them to what's actually used cuts the bill while keeping real coverage. More dashboards don't reduce metric costs, deleting all alarms blinds the team, and longer retention increases storage cost.

q: A company with 200 S3 buckets needs organization-wide visibility into storage growth, incomplete multipart uploads, and noncurrent version bloat, with actionable recommendations. Which tool provides this?
options: AWS CloudTrail
Amazon Athena
S3 Storage Lens — aggregated storage metrics, trends, and recommendations across accounts
AWS Config
explain: Storage Lens aggregates 60+ storage metrics organization-wide and flags issues like incomplete multipart uploads and version bloat with recommendations. CloudTrail audits API calls, Athena queries data rather than summarizing storage health, and Config evaluates resource configuration.

q: A finance team wants machine-learning-powered alerts on unusual spend spikes without hand-tuning static thresholds for every service. Which service provides this?
options: AWS Budgets with fixed thresholds
AWS Cost Explorer
AWS CloudTrail
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection — ML models learn normal spend patterns and alert on anomalies
explain: Cost Anomaly Detection builds per-service spend baselines with ML and alerts on deviations, no static thresholds required. Budgets need manually set thresholds, Cost Explorer is for interactive analysis rather than alerting, and CloudTrail doesn't monitor spend.

q: A company cannot attribute its EC2 and RDS spend to individual product teams, so nobody owns cost optimization. Which foundational practice enables cost allocation by team?
options: Creating a separate AWS account per resource
A consistent tagging strategy (e.g., CostCenter, Team) with cost allocation tags activated
Enabling consolidated billing alone
Setting AWS Budgets alerts
explain: Cost allocation tags flow resource spend into Cost Explorer and CUR reports grouped by team, creating ownership. Separate accounts per resource is unmanageable, consolidated billing aggregates without attributing, and Budgets alert on totals without showing who spent what.

q: An S3 bucket accumulates failed multipart uploads from clients on unreliable networks, and the abandoned parts are growing storage costs. Which lifecycle configuration cleans this up automatically?
options: A lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads after a set number of days
Enabling versioning on the bucket
Enabling cross-region replication
Transitioning objects to S3 Intelligent-Tiering
explain: The abort-incomplete-multipart-upload lifecycle action deletes orphaned parts after N days, stopping the silent storage growth. Versioning keeps more data rather than less, replication copies data, and Intelligent-Tiering optimizes complete objects — none remove abandoned upload parts.

q: Cost Explorer shows steady EBS charges even though several projects were shut down months ago. What is the MOST likely source of waste, and what is the fix?
options: EBS snapshots, which charge at full volume rates
gp3 volumes, which are the most expensive type
Unattached (available) EBS volumes — they incur full charges while detached; snapshot and delete the unneeded ones
Encrypted volumes, which cost extra per GB
explain: Detached EBS volumes bill at the full provisioned rate indefinitely, a classic leftover after project shutdowns. Snapshots bill at lower S3-backed rates, gp3 is actually the cheapest SSD option, and encryption adds no per-GB surcharge.

q: The monthly bill shows Elastic IP charges, but the team thought Elastic IPs were free. Under what condition do Elastic IPs incur charges?
options: Elastic IPs are always free regardless of use
Only when data transfers over them
Only in Regions outside us-east-1
Unassociated Elastic IPs (not attached to a running instance) incur hourly charges — release the unused ones
explain: An EIP attached to a running instance is free; idle EIPs held in the account bill hourly to discourage address hoarding. Data transfer is billed separately, and the rule applies in all Regions.

q: A DynamoDB table stores session records that become useless 30 days after creation. Manual cleanup scripts keep failing, and old items are inflating storage and scan costs. Which feature deletes expired items automatically at no extra charge?
options: Point-in-time recovery
DynamoDB TTL — automatically deletes items past their expiration timestamp free of charge
DynamoDB Streams
Adding DAX
explain: TTL deletes expired items in the background at no additional cost, eliminating both the storage bloat and the fragile cleanup scripts. PITR is for restore, Streams capture changes for processing, and DAX is a read cache — none expire data.

q: Objects in S3 Standard have not been accessed in over 2 years, but they must remain retrievable within a few hours and future access patterns are unpredictable. Which is the MOST cost-effective option?
options: Keep the objects in S3 Standard
Move everything to S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Intelligent-Tiering with Archive Access tiers enabled — automatically moves long-idle objects to low-cost archive tiers
Move everything to S3 One Zone-IA
explain: Intelligent-Tiering's Archive Access tiers automatically shift objects idle 90+ days to near-Glacier pricing while restoring within hours, ideal for unpredictable patterns. Standard overpays for cold data, Deep Archive is cheaper but takes up to 12 hours to restore, and One Zone-IA penalizes objects retrieved within 30 days and stores one copy.

q: After a reorganization, a company inherits dozens of AWS accounts full of resources nobody owns. The team needs an automated way to find idle load balancers, unassociated Elastic IPs, underutilized EC2 instances, and unattached EBS volumes across all accounts. Which tool provides these waste-finding checks?
options: Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Inspector
Amazon Macie
AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
explain: Trusted Advisor's cost optimization checks specifically hunt idle and underutilized resources — idle ELBs, unassociated EIPs, low-utilization EC2, unattached volumes. GuardDuty detects threats, Inspector scans vulnerabilities, and Macie finds sensitive data — none evaluate cost waste.

q: A team avoids daily EBS snapshots, fearing that a full copy of each volume every day will explode storage costs. What should they understand about how EBS snapshots are stored?
options: Snapshots are full copies billed at EBS volume rates
EBS snapshots are incremental — only changed blocks are stored, so daily snapshots cost little beyond the first
Snapshots cannot be automated
Snapshots are stored on the source volume itself
explain: Each snapshot stores only blocks changed since the previous one, billed at low S3-backed rates — daily snapshots are cheap insurance. They are not full copies, they are fully automatable via DLM or Backup, and they're stored in S3, not on the volume.

q: A startup serves 90% of its users from North America and Europe and wants to reduce CloudFront costs by excluding the most expensive edge locations. Which price class should it choose?
options: Price Class 100 — serves from the lowest-cost edge locations (US, Canada, Europe)
Price Class 200
Price Class All
Disabling CloudFront and serving from the origin
explain: Price Class 100 restricts delivery to the cheapest edge locations, cutting cost for a NA/EU audience. Price Class 200 adds more regions at higher cost, Price Class All uses every edge location, and dropping CloudFront sacrifices global performance rather than optimizing it.

q: A DynamoDB table on provisioned mode has stable, predictable read and write throughput, and the team expects this pattern to continue for at least a year. Which purchase lowers the table's cost?
options: Switching to on-demand mode
Adding DAX in front of the table
DynamoDB reserved capacity — commit to provisioned throughput for 1 or 3 years for a discounted rate
Enabling DynamoDB global tables
explain: Reserved capacity discounts steady provisioned throughput for a 1- or 3-year commitment, matching the predictable workload. On-demand charges a per-request premium that costs more for stable traffic, DAX adds cache cost, and global tables add replication cost.

q: A development database is actively used about 2 hours per day. The team wants the database to scale to zero and pause when idle so they pay nothing for compute overnight. Which Aurora option supports pausing?
options: Aurora provisioned clusters
Aurora Serverless v2, which scales down to 0.5 ACU but does not pause
Aurora Global Database
Aurora Serverless v1 — automatically pauses after a period of inactivity with zero compute charges
explain: Serverless v1 is the Aurora variant that pauses compute entirely after inactivity, ideal for sporadic dev use. Provisioned clusters bill 24/7, Serverless v2 scales to a 0.5 ACU minimum without pausing, and Global Database is for multi-region reads.

q: A worker polls an SQS queue every second using short polling, generating millions of empty receives that inflate the bill. Which change cuts these wasted request costs?
options: Creating additional queues
Enabling long polling — the receive call waits for messages to arrive, drastically reducing empty receives
Switching to a FIFO queue
Sending larger messages
explain: Long polling holds the ReceiveMessage call open until messages arrive or the wait expires, collapsing millions of empty polls into far fewer billed requests. More queues multiply the problem, FIFO changes ordering semantics rather than polling cost, and message size doesn't affect receive request counts.

q: A company with 15 AWS accounts wants a single bill and automatic volume discounts across all accounts. Which AWS Organizations feature provides this?
options: Consolidated billing — aggregates usage across the organization for volume discounts and one invoice
Service Control Policies
An organization CloudTrail trail
AWS Control Tower
explain: Consolidated billing pools usage across member accounts so tiered services hit volume discount thresholds sooner, with a single payer invoice. SCPs enforce guardrails, org trails centralize audit logs, and Control Tower automates landing zones — none aggregate billing.

q: A team archives 30-day log batches to S3 Glacier Deep Archive and deletes them after 60 days, but the storage bill barely drops. Why are the savings so small?
options: Retrieval fees dominate the bill
Data transfer fees dominate the bill
Glacier Deep Archive has a 180-day minimum storage charge — deleting after 60 days still bills the remaining 120 days
KMS encryption fees dominate the bill
explain: Deep Archive bills a 180-day minimum per object; early deletion charges the prorated remainder, wiping out the savings for short-lived archives. Retrieval and transfer fees apply only when data moves, and KMS charges are minor by comparison — the minimum-duration charge is the real trap.

q: A company holds existing SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance and wants to use them on EC2 instead of paying license-included rates. Which EC2 tenancy option supports this bring-your-own-license scenario?
options: Default shared tenancy
Spot Instances
RDS for SQL Server
Dedicated Hosts — required for most Microsoft BYOL scenarios under licensing terms
explain: Microsoft licensing terms generally require Dedicated Hosts for BYOL of products like SQL Server with Software Assurance. Default tenancy doesn't qualify for most BYOL, Spot is a pricing model rather than a tenancy, and RDS is license-included managed service.

q: A company enables S3 same-region replication for operational resilience. How is the replication data transfer charged compared to cross-region replication?
options: At the same rate as cross-region replication
There is no data transfer charge for same-region replication — only the storage of the replica copies
At NAT gateway data processing rates
Per-request charges replace the transfer charge
explain: S3 does not charge data transfer for replication within the same Region; you pay only for the additional storage (and requests). Cross-region replication does incur transfer charges, NAT rates are unrelated to S3 replication, and request charges apply in both cases on top.

q: A Lambda-based workload runs on x86_64 and the team wants better price-performance with no code changes. Which function setting helps?
options: Switching the instruction set architecture to arm64 (Graviton2) — better price-performance for compatible workloads
Increasing the function's memory
Extending the function timeout
Placing the function in a VPC
explain: Lambda's arm64/Graviton2 option delivers up to 34% better price-performance for most workloads with a one-line architecture change. More memory raises cost per millisecond, timeout doesn't affect unit pricing, and VPC attachment adds ENI management without price benefit.

q: A team wants AWS to automatically stop EC2 instances when forecasted spend exceeds the monthly budget, not just send an email alert. Which feature can take this automated remediation action?
options: AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Budgets alerts, which only notify
AWS Budgets Actions — can stop EC2 or RDS instances via an IAM role when a budget threshold is breached
Trusted Advisor
explain: Budgets Actions go beyond notifications: they can execute IAM-permitted actions like stopping EC2 or RDS instances when thresholds breach. Cost Explorer is analytical, standard Budgets alerts only notify, and Trusted Advisor recommends rather than acts.

q: A company is migrating a legacy order system that depends on a self-managed ActiveMQ broker. The broker must survive an AZ failure with automatic failover and no message loss, with minimal operational effort. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Amazon MQ with an active/standby multi-AZ broker deployment — failed brokers fail over automatically with messages preserved
A single-instance Amazon MQ broker
Amazon SQS standard queue
Self-managed ActiveMQ on a single EC2 instance
explain: Active/standby multi-AZ deployment synchronously replicates messages to the standby broker and fails over automatically during an AZ impairment. A single-instance broker is a single point of failure, SQS uses a different messaging API that would force an application rewrite away from JMS/ActiveMQ protocols, and self-managed ActiveMQ on one EC2 instance has no failover and full operational burden.

q: A fleet of application servers holds thousands of persistent connections to an RDS MySQL database. During Multi-AZ failover, the application suffers a long outage because every server must re-establish connections at once and DNS caches the old endpoint. Which solution minimizes application disruption during failover?
options: Increase the RDS instance size
Place RDS Proxy in front of the database — it pools connections and routes them to the new primary, preserving application connections across failover
Add RDS read replicas
Lower the DNS TTL on the RDS endpoint
explain: RDS Proxy multiplexes application connections and transparently routes them to the new primary after failover, so applications avoid the connection storm and stale-DNS window. A bigger instance doesn't change failover connection behavior, read replicas can't accept writes and don't pool connections, and a lower TTL only slightly shortens DNS caching without solving mass reconnection.

q: A company must protect 40 on-premises Windows servers with disaster recovery in AWS. The RPO must be measured in seconds and the RTO in minutes, without re-architecting the applications. Which service provides this?
options: AWS Backup
AWS DMS
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery — continuous block-level replication of servers into a low-cost staging area with rapid recovery
VM Import/Export
explain: Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates whole servers at the block level, giving second-scale RPO and minute-scale RTO for lift-and-shift recovery without application changes. AWS Backup takes scheduled backups with hour-scale RPO, DMS replicates databases rather than whole servers, and VM Import/Export is a one-time migration tool with no continuous replication.

q: A ransomware attack encrypted a company's primary data and also deleted its backups. The company needs backups that cannot be deleted or altered by anyone — including administrators — for a defined retention period. Which feature provides this?
options: S3 versioning on the backup bucket
Cross-region snapshot copies
IAM policies denying deletes
AWS Backup Vault Lock in Compliance mode — recovery points become immutable and cannot be deleted before retention expires, even by the root user
explain: Vault Lock in Compliance mode makes recovery points immutable for the retention period, so neither attackers with stolen admin credentials nor the root user can delete them early. Versioned objects can still have their versions deleted by privileged users, cross-region copies are equally deletable, and IAM deny policies can be modified by anyone with IAM permissions.

q: A company runs production workloads that depend on a Direct Connect connection to its data center. A failure of the Direct Connect location would sever connectivity. Following AWS best practices for resilient hybrid connectivity, what should the company deploy?
options: Two Direct Connect connections at different Direct Connect locations (with BFD for fast failure detection), plus a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path
A second virtual interface on the same Direct Connect connection
A larger Direct Connect connection
An internet gateway in the VPC
explain: Connections at separate locations remove the single-location failure domain, BFD detects failures in seconds, and the VPN provides an independent backup path. A second virtual interface on the same connection shares the same physical failure domain, a larger connection adds bandwidth rather than resilience, and an internet gateway doesn't connect on-premises networks.

q: A real-time multiplayer game runs active-active in two Regions behind AWS Global Accelerator. During an incident, operators need to shift 100% of traffic away from one Region in seconds, without waiting for DNS propagation. Which Global Accelerator feature enables this?
options: Route 53 failover routing
Traffic dials — adjust the percentage of traffic per endpoint group for near-instant shifts
Weighted target groups on the ALB
CloudFront origin groups
explain: Traffic dials change the traffic percentage per endpoint group almost instantly through the Global Accelerator control plane, bypassing DNS caching delays. Route 53 failover is DNS-based and subject to TTL caching, ALB weighted target groups operate within one Region rather than across Regions, and CloudFront origin groups handle HTTP failover rather than TCP game traffic.

q: A Lambda function processes SQS messages in batches of 10. When one message in a batch fails, the entire batch is retried, causing the 9 successful messages to be reprocessed. How can the function avoid reprocessing successful messages?
options: Increase the batch size
Delete the queue and recreate it
Enable ReportBatchItemFailures (partial batch responses) so only failed message IDs are returned for retry
Set the visibility timeout to zero
explain: Partial batch responses let the function report exactly which message IDs failed, so only those return to the queue instead of the whole batch. A larger batch makes the reprocessing worse, recreating the queue loses in-flight messages, and a zero visibility timeout causes constant duplicate delivery.

q: During an origin outage, a CloudFront-backed site shows the origin's raw 500 error page. The company wants CloudFront to serve a branded maintenance page from S3 during origin errors and to cache that error response briefly so the origin isn't hammered. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: An origin group with the ALB as primary
Lambda@Edge on viewer request
Longer default TTLs on all content
CloudFront custom error responses — return a branded page from S3 for 5xx errors with a short error caching minimum TTL
explain: Custom error responses substitute a branded page for origin error codes and the error caching TTL keeps CloudFront from retrying the failing origin on every request. Origin groups fail over to a backup origin rather than serving a static page, Lambda@Edge on viewer request runs before origin errors occur, and long TTLs would cache stale dynamic content rather than handling errors.

q: After each deployment, newly registered targets receive full traffic immediately and return errors while their caches warm up. Which ALB target group feature ramps traffic to new targets gradually?
options: Slow start mode — gradually increases traffic to newly registered targets over a configurable warm-up period
Sticky sessions
Deregistration delay
Cross-zone load balancing
explain: Slow start ramps traffic to new targets linearly over the warm-up duration, giving caches time to fill before full load arrives. Sticky sessions pin users to targets without ramping, deregistration delay only affects how long draining takes when targets are removed, and cross-zone balancing spreads traffic across AZs without any warm-up behavior.

q: An Auto Scaling group launches instances that need 6 minutes to install software and pass application health checks. The load balancer marks them unhealthy at minute 2 and terminates them, so the group never stabilizes. What should be changed?
options: Disable health checks
Increase the health check grace period beyond the 6-minute boot time so instances can initialize before health evaluation
Decrease the cooldown period
Set the minimum group size to zero
explain: The grace period suspends health-check-driven termination while instances boot; it must exceed the worst-case initialization time. Disabling health checks removes all failure detection, the cooldown period governs scaling activity pacing rather than health evaluation, and a zero minimum doesn't stop premature termination of booting instances.

q: A company is designing for a regional control-plane impairment during which Auto Scaling launches might fail. Which design principle keeps the workload available even if scaling actions cannot run?
options: Rely on target tracking to add capacity during the event
Run everything in a single AZ
Static stability — pre-provision enough minimum capacity across AZs to handle expected load without depending on scaling during the event
Use scheduled scaling to add capacity when the event starts
explain: Static stability means the steady-state deployment already carries the load, so an impaired scaling control plane doesn't cause an outage. Target tracking and scheduled scaling both depend on the control plane that is impaired, and a single AZ concentrates rather than distributes risk.

q: Before a major product launch, a team wants to validate that its multi-AZ architecture actually survives an AZ failure — without causing a real outage. Which service runs controlled fault-injection experiments against AWS resources?
options: AWS Config
CloudWatch Synthetics
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Fault Injection Simulator — injects faults like AZ impairment in a controlled, guardrailed experiment
explain: Fault Injection Simulator runs game-day style experiments with blast-radius guardrails and automatic rollback, proving resilience before a real failure. Config evaluates resource compliance, Synthetics monitors user flows rather than injecting faults, and Trusted Advisor reports best-practice checks without testing failure behavior.

q: A checkout flow depends on five microservices. Individual service health checks are green, yet customers report checkout failures. The team needs monitoring that exercises the full user journey from outside the application. Which solution provides this?
options: CloudWatch Synthetics canaries — scripted browser/API checks that run the checkout flow continuously and alert on failure
VPC Flow Logs
More granular CloudWatch alarms per service
AWS X-Ray sampling
explain: Synthetics canaries simulate real user transactions end to end, catching integration failures that per-service health checks miss. Flow Logs show packet metadata rather than user journeys, more per-service alarms still can't see cross-service breakage, and X-Ray traces real traffic but doesn't proactively exercise the flow.

q: A gaming company is launching a popular title and expects large volumetric DDoS attacks against its login API behind an ALB. Which combination provides the MOST comprehensive protection?
options: Security groups with rate limiting
CloudFront + AWS WAF + Shield Advanced in front of the ALB — edge absorption, Layer 7 filtering, and DDoS response team with cost protection
A NAT gateway in each AZ
ElastiCache in front of the API
explain: The layered combination absorbs volumetric attacks at the edge, filters application-layer abuse, and adds the DDoS Response Team plus cost protection during attacks. Security groups can't rate-limit, NAT gateways only serve outbound traffic, and a cache doesn't absorb or filter attack traffic.

q: A company keeps database backups in an S3 bucket in its production account. An attacker who compromises production credentials could delete the backups. Which design keeps restorable copies even if the production account is fully compromised?
options: Versioning on the production bucket
A lifecycle policy to Glacier
Replicate backups to a bucket in a separate security account with Object Lock Compliance mode and a bucket policy denying deletes
S3 server access logging
explain: Copies in a separate account sit outside the compromised credential boundary, and Object Lock Compliance mode makes them immutable even to that account's root user. Versioning doesn't help when the attacker can delete versions, lifecycle transitions don't prevent deletion, and access logging is detective rather than protective.

q: An Aurora PostgreSQL cluster is growing rapidly and the team fears an outage if storage fills up. How does Aurora handle storage capacity as data grows?
options: The DBA must add storage manually
Storage is fixed at cluster creation
Enable RDS storage autoscaling
Aurora storage auto-scales from 10 GB up to 128 TB in 10 GB increments with no action required
explain: Aurora's distributed storage layer grows automatically in 10 GB increments as data grows, so there is no full-disk outage scenario to manage. Manual storage management isn't needed, storage isn't fixed at creation, and RDS storage autoscaling is a separate feature for non-Aurora RDS instances.

q: A real-time bidding platform needs sub-millisecond data access with strong durability: no data loss on node failure, Multi-AZ failover, and no separate persistence layer to manage. ElastiCache for Redis with replicas doesn't meet the durability bar. Which service is purpose-built for this?
options: Amazon MemoryDB for Redis — durable in-memory database with Multi-AZ transactional log persistence
ElastiCache for Memcached
DynamoDB with DAX
RDS for MySQL
explain: MemoryDB persists every write to a Multi-AZ transactional log, giving Redis-speed reads with database-grade durability and fast failover. Memcached offers no persistence or replication, DAX is a cache in front of DynamoDB rather than a durable primary store, and RDS delivers millisecond rather than sub-millisecond latency.

q: An EventBridge rule invokes a Lambda function for each order event. When the function is throttled, some invocations fail and the events disappear after retries are exhausted. How can failed invocations be captured?
options: Increase the Lambda timeout
Configure a dead-letter queue on the EventBridge rule target — failed invocations are sent to SQS after retry exhaustion
Enable EventBridge Scheduler
Add more Lambda concurrency
explain: A DLQ on the rule target captures events that fail all retries, preserving them for analysis and redrive. Timeout changes don't capture failures, Scheduler creates new scheduled events rather than preserving failed ones, and more concurrency reduces throttling but still loses events when failures occur.

q: An SNS topic fans out to an HTTPS endpoint and an SQS queue. The HTTPS endpoint goes down for maintenance each night and misses notifications. Which configuration ensures the endpoint eventually receives the missed messages without code changes?
options: Delete and recreate the subscription daily
Increase the SNS message size
SNS delivery retry policies with backoff plus a dead-letter queue on the subscription for messages that exhaust retries
Replace SNS with SQS FIFO
explain: Delivery retry policies redeliver with backoff across the maintenance window, and the subscription DLQ preserves anything that still fails for later redrive. Recreating the subscription loses messages, message size is irrelevant to delivery failures, and replacing SNS with SQS FIFO changes the architecture instead of fixing delivery.

q: A company uses Route 53 weighted routing to split traffic 70/30 between two Regions. During an outage in the primary Region, users are still sent there and see errors. The weights were never changed. What is the likely misconfiguration?
options: Weighted routing doesn't support failover
The TTL is too low
Geolocation routing should have been used
No health checks are attached to the weighted records — Route 53 only removes unhealthy endpoints from responses when health checks are configured
explain: Without health checks, Route 53 has no failure signal and keeps returning the impaired endpoint per the weights; health checks let it exclude unhealthy records automatically. Weighted routing does support health-based exclusion, a low TTL would speed rather than prevent failover, and geolocation routing without health checks has the same blind spot.

q: A company is migrating Windows file shares that require the SMB protocol and Active Directory integration. The file system must remain available during an AZ outage with automatic failover. Which FSx deployment meets this requirement?
options: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with the Multi-AZ deployment type — synchronous replication with automatic failover
FSx for Windows File Server Single-AZ
Amazon EFS
FSx for Lustre
explain: The Multi-AZ deployment type keeps a synchronous standby and fails over automatically, delivering Windows-native SMB with AD integration. Single-AZ goes down with its AZ, EFS speaks NFS rather than SMB and lacks Windows AD integration, and FSx for Lustre is a POSIX HPC file system.

q: A team deploys a containerized payment service to ECS. A bad deployment last month caused an outage because the new version replaced the old one with no quick way back. Which deployment strategy provisions the new version alongside the old and shifts traffic only after validation, with automatic rollback on failure?
options: Rolling update replacing all tasks at once
CodeDeploy blue/green deployment for ECS — new (green) task set validated behind a test listener before traffic shifts, with automatic rollback
Manual task replacement via the console
Deploying with maximum 200% and minimum 0%
explain: Blue/green keeps the proven blue task set serving traffic while the green set is validated, then shifts listeners over and rolls back automatically if alarms fire. A full rolling replacement offers no safe harbor, console replacement is slow and manual, and min/max percentages alone don't validate before shifting traffic.

q: A global gaming company runs Redis on ElastiCache in us-east-1. Players in Asia-Pacific suffer high latency, and a regional outage would lose the leaderboard. The data must be readable with low latency in both Regions with cross-region replication lag under a second. Which solution meets this?
options: A single Redis cluster with larger nodes
DynamoDB global tables
ElastiCache Global Datastore — cross-region replication with active-passive clusters and typical lag under one second
Redis read replicas in the same Region
explain: Global Datastore replicates the ElastiCache cluster cross-region with sub-second lag, giving local reads in both Regions and a regional failover target. Bigger nodes don't shorten intercontinental distance, DynamoDB global tables would force a data-model rewrite away from Redis APIs, and same-Region replicas don't address latency or regional outages.

q: A company must keep two copies of critical objects in the same Region for operational recovery — if an application corrupts the primary bucket, the team restores from the second bucket. Cross-region transfer costs are a concern. Which replication approach is MOST cost-effective?
options: Cross-region replication to another Region
Manual daily copies with the CLI
S3 Batch Replication on a schedule
S3 Same-Region Replication — automatic ongoing copies with no data transfer charge within the Region
explain: Same-Region Replication copies new objects automatically with no inter-region transfer charge, paying only for the replica storage. Cross-region replication incurs transfer fees, manual CLI copies are toil-heavy and error-prone, and Batch Replication is a one-time backfill job rather than ongoing protection.

q: An application runs behind a Network Load Balancer across three AZs. One AZ experiences partial impairment, but the application stays up in the other two. Operators want to shift traffic away from the impaired AZ in seconds without changing DNS or scaling. Which feature provides this?
options: Route 53 Application Recovery Controller zonal shift — shifts traffic away from an AZ for supported resources in seconds
Route 53 failover routing
Deregistering targets manually
Terminating all instances in the impaired AZ
explain: Zonal shift moves traffic off an impaired AZ through the ARC control plane in seconds with no DNS changes. Failover routing is DNS-based and slower, manual deregistration is toil-heavy across many targets, and terminating instances destroys capacity that will be needed when the AZ recovers.

q: A trading application stores market data in S3 Standard in a single AZ and needs single-digit millisecond GET/PUT latency. The application runs entirely in the same AZ and can tolerate AZ-scoped durability for this cacheable dataset. Which storage class delivers the lowest latency?
options: S3 Standard
S3 Express One Zone — single-digit millisecond data access for latency-sensitive workloads in one AZ
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 Standard-IA
explain: S3 Express One Zone keeps data in a single AZ on high-performance hardware, delivering consistent single-digit millisecond access for workloads co-located in that AZ. S3 Standard has higher request latency, Glacier Instant Retrieval is an archive class with millisecond (not single-digit millisecond) retrieval, and Standard-IA is priced for infrequent access rather than speed.

q: A video-on-demand service streams from EBS-backed origin servers. The workload needs 800 MB/s of sustained sequential throughput but only 4,000 IOPS per volume. With gp2, the team would have to massively over-provision volume size to reach the throughput. Which volume configuration meets the throughput need at the lowest cost?
options: io2 Block Express
st1 Throughput Optimized HDD
gp3 with provisioned throughput up to 1,000 MB/s — throughput provisioned independently of IOPS and size
Larger gp2 volumes
explain: gp3 decouples throughput from IOPS and capacity, so the team can dial up to 1,000 MB/s without paying for unneeded IOPS or terabytes of capacity. io2 is priced for extreme IOPS that this workload doesn't need, a single st1 volume tops out below 800 MB/s, and larger gp2 volumes bundle IOPS and throughput together wastefully.

q: A log-processing cluster performs large sequential scans of 50 TB of log data staged on EBS. IOPS don't matter; only streaming throughput per dollar. Which is the MOST cost-effective volume type?
options: io2
gp3 with provisioned IOPS
EBS Snapshots
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) — lowest cost per MB/s for sequential throughput workloads
explain: st1 is purpose-built for big sequential scans, delivering high streaming throughput at HDD prices — the cheapest MB/s of any EBS type. io2 and provisioned-IOPS gp3 charge premium prices for IOPS this workload never uses, and snapshots are point-in-time backups, not live volumes.

q: A Redis cache holds 800 GB of session data but only 20% is accessed frequently. The team is paying for all-RAM nodes. Which ElastiCache option keeps hot data in memory and spills colder data to SSD at lower cost?
options: Redis data tiering on r6gd nodes — automatically tiers infrequently accessed data to local NVMe SSDs
More read replicas
Memcached
Larger RAM-only nodes
explain: Data tiering keeps frequently accessed keys in memory while colder data lives on local NVMe SSDs, cutting the cost per GB for large datasets with skewed access. Read replicas add more RAM cost without tiering, Memcached has no tiering or persistence, and larger RAM-only nodes just scale the same expensive pattern.

q: A nightly ETL job must export a 500 GB DynamoDB table to S3. A single-threaded Scan takes 8 hours and the window is 2 hours. Which approach parallelizes the export?
options: Increase provisioned read capacity only
Parallel scans with multiple segments — divide the table into segments scanned concurrently
Enable DynamoDB Streams
Add a global secondary index
explain: Parallel scans split the table into logical segments that workers scan simultaneously, multiplying throughput across the fleet. More read capacity helps but a single-threaded scan still can't use it, Streams capture ongoing changes rather than bulk-exporting, and a GSI adds an alternate query pattern without parallelizing full exports.

q: Athena queries over 5 TB of CSV logs in S3 are slow and expensive. Queries filter on a few columns and aggregate by day. Which change gives the BIGGEST improvement in both speed and cost?
options: Use a larger workgroup
Enable Transfer Acceleration
Convert the data to Parquet (columnar) format and partition by date — Athena scans only needed columns and partitions
Move the data to S3 Standard-IA
explain: Parquet's columnar layout means Athena reads only the referenced columns, and date partitioning prunes irrelevant prefixes — together slashing scanned bytes, which is what Athena bills on. Workgroup size doesn't reduce scanned data, Transfer Acceleration affects upload speed, and the storage class doesn't change how much Athena scans.

q: A Redshift cluster runs slow joins between a 2 TB fact table and dimension tables. Data is distributed EVENLY, so every join redistributes rows across nodes. Which design change minimizes data movement during joins?
options: Add more nodes
Enable concurrency scaling
Take more frequent snapshots
Use KEY distribution on the join key for the fact table and ALL distribution for small dimensions, with sort keys on filter columns
explain: KEY distribution co-locates matching join rows on the same node, ALL distribution replicates small dimensions everywhere, and sort keys let Redshift skip unsorted blocks — together eliminating most redistribution. More nodes don't fix a bad distribution strategy, concurrency scaling adds burst query capacity rather than join efficiency, and snapshots are for recovery.

q: An EMR cluster using a single Spot instance type frequently fails to scale because that capacity pool is exhausted. Which EMR configuration improves the odds of obtaining capacity during scale-out?
options: Instance fleets with multiple instance types across AZs — EMR provisions from whichever pools have capacity
Instance groups with one fixed instance type
Larger core nodes
On-Demand only for all nodes
explain: Instance fleets let EMR pick from many instance types and AZs, so an exhausted pool just means provisioning from another. Fixed instance groups concentrate on one pool, larger nodes share the same pool risk, and all-On-Demand abandons Spot savings without guaranteeing capacity either.

q: AWS Glue ETL jobs process data volumes that vary 20x day to day. Engineers manually tune the number of DPUs per job and constantly get it wrong — jobs are slow or wasteful. Which feature adjusts Glue capacity automatically?
options: Glue DataBrew
AWS Glue Auto Scaling — monitors the job and adjusts DPUs dynamically
