Fixed maximum DPUs on every job
Running jobs on a schedule only
explain: Glue Auto Scaling adds and removes workers based on the job's actual parallelism needs, handling 20x variance without manual tuning. DataBrew is a visual data-prep tool, fixed maximum DPUs waste money on small days, and scheduling changes when jobs run rather than how they're sized.

q: A Kinesis data stream ingests clickstream data with unpredictable viral spikes. Provisioning shards for the peak wastes money; provisioning for the average throttles during spikes. Which capacity mode handles this without shard management?
options: Provisioned mode with fixed shards
Fewer shards with enhanced fan-out
On-demand mode — automatically scales ingest throughput with traffic, pay per GB
Shorter retention period
explain: On-demand mode scales stream throughput automatically with traffic and bills per GB ingested, eliminating shard math for spiky workloads. Fixed provisioned shards recreate the original dilemma, enhanced fan-out scales consumer read throughput rather than ingest, and retention period doesn't change throughput capacity.

q: A Lambda function downloads a 6 GB machine learning model to /tmp for inference, but /tmp is limited to 512 MB by default and the function fails. Which change gives the function enough scratch space?
options: Increase the function memory to 10 GB
Attach an EBS volume
Use Lambda SnapStart
Configure ephemeral storage up to 10 GB — expands /tmp for data-intensive functions
explain: Ephemeral storage can be raised to 10 GB, expanding /tmp for model files and intermediate data. Memory controls CPU and heap rather than /tmp size, EBS volumes can't attach to Lambda, and SnapStart reduces cold-start latency without adding storage.

q: A compute-bound Lambda function runs slowly at 512 MB. The team assumes more memory only raises cost. What should they understand about Lambda's CPU allocation?
options: CPU scales proportionally with memory — increasing memory adds vCPU and can reduce duration enough to lower total cost
CPU is fixed regardless of memory
Only timeout affects duration
VPC-attached functions get more CPU
explain: Lambda allocates CPU power in proportion to configured memory, so compute-bound functions often finish dramatically faster at higher memory — and the shorter duration can more than offset the higher per-millisecond rate. CPU is not fixed, timeout caps duration rather than speeding execution, and VPC attachment doesn't change CPU allocation.

q: An EKS cluster runs spiky batch pods. The Cluster Autoscaler takes minutes to provision right-sized nodes, and bin-packing is inefficient. Which provisioner launches just-in-time, right-sized nodes in seconds based on pending pod requirements?
options: Managed node groups with fixed sizes
Karpenter — observes pending pods and provisions optimal nodes in seconds
Fargate profiles for everything
Larger static nodes
explain: Karpenter watches unschedulable pods and provisions precisely-sized nodes directly, reacting in seconds with far better bin-packing than autoscaling groups. Fixed node groups scale slowly in coarse increments, Fargate is a different serverless compute model, and larger static nodes waste money between spikes.

q: A gRPC service behind an ALB has long-lived connections. The default round-robin routing sends new streams to targets that are already saturated, while others sit idle. Which ALB routing algorithm accounts for in-flight requests?
options: Round robin
Sticky sessions
Least outstanding requests — routes to the target with the fewest in-flight requests
Weighted target groups
explain: Least outstanding requests considers active request counts, which is the right signal for long-lived gRPC streams where connection count doesn't reflect load. Round robin ignores load entirely, sticky sessions pin clients without balancing, and weighted target groups use static weights rather than live load.

q: A company must inspect all VPC internet-bound traffic with third-party firewall appliances. As traffic grows, the single appliance pair becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Which load balancer transparently scales and distributes traffic across a fleet of appliances?
options: Application Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer — distributes traffic to virtual appliances transparently with automatic scaling and failover
explain: Gateway Load Balancer chains traffic through appliance fleets transparently using GENEVE encapsulation, scaling appliances horizontally with built-in health checks and failover. ALB routes HTTP rather than transparently inserting appliances, NLB doesn't do appliance chaining, and Classic is legacy.

q: A team is building a simple Lambda-proxy API with JWT authorization. They don't need REST API features like request/response transformations or caching. Which API Gateway option offers lower latency and lower cost for this use case?
options: HTTP APIs — cheaper and lower-latency for proxy integrations with JWT authorizer support
REST APIs
WebSocket APIs
Private REST APIs
explain: HTTP APIs are purpose-built for Lambda-proxy workloads with native JWT authorizers, delivering lower latency at a lower price than REST APIs. REST APIs add features (and cost) this workload doesn't use, WebSocket APIs serve bidirectional messaging rather than request/response, and private APIs address network isolation rather than cost.

q: A startup wants to run a containerized web service that scales automatically with traffic, with no cluster or load balancer to manage and pay-as-you-go pricing. Which service is the simplest fit?
options: EKS with managed node groups
AWS App Runner — fully managed container web service with automatic scaling
EC2 with Auto Scaling
AWS Batch
explain: App Runner takes a container image or code and runs it as an auto-scaling web service with a built-in load balancer — no clusters, node groups, or scaling policies to manage. EKS and EC2 Auto Scaling both require cluster/infrastructure management, and Batch schedules batch jobs rather than serving web traffic.

q: An application downloads 30 GB model files from S3 over high-bandwidth links, but a single GET tops out well below the available bandwidth. Which technique maximizes full-file download throughput?
options: S3 Transfer Acceleration
Multipart upload
Parallel byte-range GET requests — download object parts concurrently and reassemble
S3 Select
explain: Issuing multiple ranged GETs in parallel saturates the available bandwidth and reassembles the full object client-side, far exceeding single-connection throughput. Transfer Acceleration optimizes the internet path rather than per-connection throughput, multipart upload applies to uploads, and S3 Select retrieves filtered subsets rather than full files faster.

q: A hybrid application replicates large datasets between an on-premises data center and AWS nightly. Over the internet VPN, throughput varies wildly and transfers miss their window. Which connectivity option provides consistent, dedicated network performance?
options: A larger VPN tunnel
S3 Transfer Acceleration
An internet gateway with bigger instances
AWS Direct Connect — dedicated private connection with consistent bandwidth
explain: Direct Connect provides dedicated private bandwidth that doesn't vary with internet congestion, giving predictable transfer windows. A bigger VPN tunnel still rides the variable public internet, Transfer Acceleration optimizes S3 upload paths rather than providing consistent private throughput, and instance size doesn't fix internet variability.

q: A company runs 5 critical ZooKeeper nodes that must each sit on distinct underlying hardware in different racks to survive correlated hardware failures. Which placement group spreads a small number of instances across distinct hardware?
options: Spread placement group — places each instance on distinct racks (max 7 per AZ)
Cluster placement group
Partition placement group
No placement group
explain: Spread placement puts each instance on separate racks, so a rack-level failure takes down at most one node — ideal for small critical fleets like ZooKeeper. Cluster placement packs instances together for low latency (the opposite goal), partition placement targets large distributed systems like HDFS, and no placement group gives no hardware-separation guarantees.

q: An Aurora cluster serves transactional readers and heavy analytics readers from the same reader endpoint. Analytics queries saturate replicas and slow down the application. How can the team isolate the two workloads without adding clusters?
options: Increase the writer instance size
Create a custom endpoint pinned to specific replicas for analytics, keeping the default reader endpoint for transactional reads
Enable Multi-AZ
Add the analytics queries to the writer
explain: Custom endpoints let the team dedicate certain replicas to analytics while transactional reads use the remaining replicas, isolating the noisy workload. A bigger writer doesn't separate reader load, Multi-AZ addresses failover rather than workload isolation, and running analytics on the writer would hurt write performance.

q: A CloudFront distribution serves an API where responses vary by an Authorization header and a few query parameters. The cache hit ratio is near zero because the cache key includes every query string. Which change improves the hit ratio without serving wrong content?
options: Cache everything with a 24-hour TTL
Disable caching for the API
Tune the cache policy to include only the query parameters and headers that actually change the response
Use signed URLs for all requests
explain: Including only the varying parameters and headers in the cache key collapses redundant cache entries while still differentiating genuinely different responses. A blanket long TTL would serve one user's personalized response to another, disabling caching forfeits performance, and signed URLs control access rather than cache keys.

q: A product catalog changes a few times per day and is read thousands of times per second. Stale data for a few minutes after a change is acceptable. Which ElastiCache strategy minimizes database load with the least complexity?
options: Write-through caching
No caching
Cache-aside with immediate invalidation on every write
Lazy loading (cache-aside) with a TTL — populate on miss, expire entries so changes appear within minutes
explain: Lazy loading with a TTL is the simplest pattern: misses populate the cache and expirations bound staleness to minutes, matching the tolerance. Write-through adds synchronous write complexity needed only when staleness is unacceptable, no caching leaves the database absorbing full read load, and immediate invalidation adds coordination the staleness budget doesn't require.

q: A DynamoDB-backed dashboard reads the same items repeatedly and is tolerant of slightly stale data. Read costs are high. Which read option halves the read capacity consumed per request?
options: Eventually consistent reads — the default, consuming half the RCUs of strongly consistent reads
Strongly consistent reads
DAX
Global secondary index
explain: Eventually consistent reads (the DynamoDB default) consume half the read capacity units of strongly consistent reads — an easy win when slight staleness is acceptable. Strongly consistent reads cost double, DAX is a caching layer that doesn't change the read pricing model, and a GSI carries its own provisioned throughput rather than cheaper reads.

q: A producer sends 5 million small messages per day to SQS with one SendMessage call each. API request charges are significant. Which change reduces the number of billed SQS API requests?
options: Long polling
SendMessageBatch — group up to 10 messages per API call
FIFO queue
Larger visibility timeout
explain: SendMessageBatch packs up to 10 messages into one API call, cutting producer request charges by up to 10x. Long polling reduces empty receives on the consumer side rather than producer sends, FIFO changes ordering semantics rather than request counts, and visibility timeout affects redelivery timing.

q: A SaaS vendor needs read-only access to a customer's S3 bucket. The customer creates a role the vendor can assume. To prevent another customer of the same vendor from using that role (the confused deputy problem), what should the customer require in the role's trust policy?
options: A permissions boundary
MFA on the vendor's IAM users
An External ID condition — a secret value the vendor must present that is unique per customer
A bucket policy allowing the vendor's account
explain: The External ID is a per-customer secret the vendor must include when assuming the role, so one customer can't be tricked into acting for another. A permissions boundary caps the role's maximum permissions without authenticating which customer is calling, MFA on the vendor's users doesn't bind the assumption to the right customer, and an account-level bucket policy still can't distinguish between the vendor's customers.

q: Compliance requires that all access to a sensitive S3 bucket use TLS — plaintext HTTP requests must be rejected even if the requester has valid permissions. Which bucket policy approach enforces this?
options: S3 Block Public Access
A VPC endpoint policy
SSE-KMS encryption
A bucket policy with an explicit deny on s3:* when aws:SecureTransport is false
explain: An explicit deny keyed on the aws:SecureTransport condition rejects any request not made over TLS, regardless of the caller's other permissions. Block Public Access controls public exposure rather than the transport protocol, VPC endpoint policies govern the network path rather than TLS, and SSE-KMS encrypts data at rest rather than in transit.

q: Applications in private subnets access S3 through a VPC gateway endpoint. The security team wants the bucket to reject any request that doesn't arrive through the company's VPC endpoints, even from valid IAM principals. Which condition key enforces this?
options: aws:SourceVpce — deny requests whose source VPC endpoint doesn't match the company's endpoint IDs
aws:SourceIp
aws:PrincipalAccount
s3:x-amz-acl
explain: aws:SourceVpce identifies the VPC endpoint a request traveled through, so the bucket policy can deny anything not arriving via the approved endpoints. Source IP is unreliable for this because private addresses aren't visible at the bucket, PrincipalAccount restricts which account calls rather than the network path, and s3:x-amz-acl governs canned ACLs on writes rather than request origin.

q: A KMS key is used only for S3 server-side encryption. The security team wants the key to be unusable if called directly — it must only work when the request comes through the S3 service. Which key policy condition enforces this?
options: kms:CallerAccount
kms:ViaService — allow only when the request is made via s3.<region>.amazonaws.com
aws:SecureTransport
Automatic key rotation
explain: kms:ViaService constrains the key so it only works when the call arrives through the specified AWS service, preventing direct misuse of the key. CallerAccount restricts which account calls rather than the service path, SecureTransport governs TLS rather than service routing, and automatic rotation manages key lifecycle rather than authorization scope.

q: A company shares an encrypted EBS snapshot with a partner account, but the partner gets AccessDenied when creating a volume from it. The snapshot share itself succeeded. What is missing?
options: The snapshot must be unencrypted
A larger volume size
The partner needs permission on the KMS key — share the customer managed key (or re-encrypt a copy with a shared key) and grant the partner's account access
VPC peering between accounts
explain: Encrypted snapshots can only be used by principals authorized on the KMS key; sharing the snapshot alone is insufficient, so the key must also be shared with the partner account. Unencrypting the snapshot would destroy the security posture, volume size is irrelevant to authorization, and VPC peering has nothing to do with snapshot permissions.

q: A fleet of EC2 instances connects to RDS for MySQL using a shared database password stored in config files. The security team wants passwordless authentication with short-lived tokens tied to IAM identities. Which feature provides this?
options: Secrets Manager rotation
Longer passwords
Security groups
RDS IAM database authentication — applications request short-lived auth tokens using IAM credentials
explain: IAM database authentication lets applications generate time-limited auth tokens signed with IAM credentials, eliminating stored passwords entirely. Secrets Manager rotation improves password hygiene but still uses passwords, longer passwords don't remove the shared-secret problem, and security groups control network access rather than database authentication.

q: A Redis cluster on ElastiCache holds session tokens. The security team requires encryption in transit and at rest, plus authentication for every client connection. Which configuration meets all three?
options: Enable encryption in transit, encryption at rest, and Redis AUTH tokens on the replication group
Memcached with SASL
Security groups only
Larger node types
explain: The ElastiCache Redis replication group supports TLS in transit, at-rest encryption, and AUTH tokens together, covering all three requirements. Memcached lacks at-rest encryption and Redis-style auth tokens, security groups only filter network traffic without encrypting or authenticating it, and node size has no security effect.

q: A company runs Amazon MSK and wants Kafka client authentication integrated with IAM — no long-lived SCRAM secrets to rotate, with fine-grained topic-level permissions. Which MSK authentication option provides this?
options: Unauthenticated access with open security groups
IAM access control for MSK — SASL/OAUTHBEARER with IAM, authorized via Kafka ACLs mapped to IAM identities
TLS without client authentication
Storing SCRAM secrets in application code
explain: IAM access control lets Kafka clients authenticate with short-lived IAM credentials and enforces topic-level permissions through Kafka ACLs tied to IAM identities. Unauthenticated access with open security groups is the vulnerability being fixed, TLS alone encrypts without authenticating clients, and hardcoded SCRAM secrets are exactly the operational burden to eliminate.

q: Management events in CloudTrail show who changed a bucket policy, but the audit team also needs a record of who read or wrote individual objects in a highly sensitive bucket. Which CloudTrail configuration captures object-level activity?
options: Log file integrity validation
S3 server access logging
Enable CloudTrail data events for S3 object-level operations on the bucket
VPC Flow Logs
explain: CloudTrail data events record object-level API calls like GetObject and PutObject, which management events omit by default. Log file validation detects tampering rather than adding event types, S3 server access logging is a separate bucket-level mechanism rather than a CloudTrail configuration, and Flow Logs capture network metadata rather than S3 API calls.

q: After a security incident, responders need to know which internal hosts communicated with a suspicious external IP and on which ports, over the past 30 days. Which data source provides this network-level history?
options: CloudTrail management events
DNS query logs
Application logs only
VPC Flow Logs — captured IP traffic metadata (source, destination, ports, bytes) for the VPC
explain: Flow Logs record source, destination, ports, packet and byte counts for VPC traffic, giving responders the connection history they need. CloudTrail logs API calls rather than packet flows, DNS logs show queried domains rather than IP/port conversations, and application logs give an incomplete, app-specific view of network activity.

q: EC2 instances must resolve external domains for updates, but the security team wants to block DNS queries to known malicious domains across the entire VPC. Which service filters outbound DNS at the Resolver level?
options: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall — domain lists with allow/block rules applied to VPC DNS queries
Security groups
NACLs
AWS WAF
explain: Resolver DNS Firewall inspects DNS queries leaving the VPC and blocks domains on a denylist before resolution completes. Security groups and NACLs filter by IP and port rather than domain names, and WAF inspects HTTP requests rather than DNS traffic.

q: Users upload files to an S3 bucket that are later processed by backend systems. The security team wants every uploaded object scanned for malware without managing scanning infrastructure. Which feature provides this?
options: S3 versioning
GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 — scans new objects on upload and tags/quarantines findings
Macie
S3 Object Lock
explain: Malware Protection for S3 automatically scans objects on upload using managed scanning infrastructure and surfaces findings for quarantine workflows. Versioning aids recovery rather than scanning, Macie discovers sensitive data rather than malware, and Object Lock enforces immutability without inspecting content.

q: A company deploys dozens of Lambda functions and wants continuous scanning of function code and dependencies for known vulnerabilities, without adding agents. Which service covers Lambda in its assessments?
options: GuardDuty
AWS WAF
Amazon Inspector — assesses Lambda functions and layers for software vulnerabilities
CloudTrail Insights
explain: Inspector continuously scans Lambda function code and layers for CVEs in application dependencies, agentless. GuardDuty detects threats from logs rather than scanning code for vulnerabilities, WAF filters web requests, and CloudTrail Insights flags anomalous API activity.

q: A Config rule flags S3 buckets that become publicly accessible, but remediation depends on an engineer noticing the alert. The team wants non-compliant buckets fixed automatically within minutes. Which approach provides this?
options: More CloudWatch alarms
AWS Budgets Actions
Manual runbooks
AWS Config auto-remediation with an SSM Automation document — triggers a corrective action when the rule goes non-compliant
explain: Config auto-remediation invokes an SSM Automation document the moment a resource goes non-compliant, closing the exposure without human delay. More alarms still require a human responder, Budgets Actions act on cost thresholds rather than configuration drift, and manual runbooks are the slow process being replaced.

q: A ticketing site is overrun by sophisticated bots that rotate user agents, solve simple challenges, and mimic human browsing. Standard rate-based rules aren't stopping them. Which WAF managed rule group is purpose-built for this?
options: AWSManagedRulesBotControlRuleSet — detects and manages sophisticated bot traffic with bot signatures and machine learning
AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet
Geo match rules
IP reputation lists alone
explain: The Bot Control rule group uses AWS threat intelligence and ML to identify evasive bots that defeat simple heuristics. The SQLi rule group targets injection payloads rather than bots, geo match blocks whole countries instead of bot behavior, and static IP lists are evaded by the rotating IPs these bots use.

q: A login form faces credential-stuffing attempts. The team wants suspicious requests to face an interactive proof-of-humanity instead of being silently blocked, to avoid locking out real users caught by heuristics. Which WAF action provides this?
options: Block
CAPTCHA or Challenge actions — present a puzzle or silent browser check before allowing the request
Count
Rate-based rule with block
explain: CAPTCHA and Challenge actions verify humanness interactively, letting legitimate users through while stopping automated stuffing. Silent Block risks false positives against real users, Count only logs without acting, and a rate-based block has the same false-positive problem as a plain block.

q: An audit found IAM roles with permissions granted a year ago that were never used. The team wants findings that identify unused permissions so policies can be tightened to least privilege. Which feature generates these findings?
options: IAM credential report
CloudTrail Insights
IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings — identifies unused roles, keys, and permissions
Trusted Advisor
explain: Access Analyzer's unused access analysis compares granted permissions against actual usage and flags what's safe to remove. The credential report shows credential age rather than permission usage, CloudTrail Insights flags anomalous API bursts rather than unused grants, and Trusted Advisor's IAM checks don't produce unused-permission findings.

q: A company wants a guardrail ensuring IAM users cannot perform sensitive actions (like IAM changes) without having authenticated with MFA — enforced centrally so no account can opt out. Which control provides this?
options: An IAM policy on each user
A strong password policy
AWS Budgets
An SCP denying sensitive actions when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false — applies organization-wide
explain: An SCP with the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition centrally denies sensitive actions for non-MFA sessions across every account, and member accounts can't override it. Per-user IAM policies drift and can be edited locally, password policies don't enforce MFA, and Budgets monitor spend rather than access control.

q: A company with 50 accounts wants GuardDuty and Security Hub enabled everywhere with findings aggregated centrally, managed by the security team without using the management account for daily operations. Which Organizations feature enables this?
options: Delegated administrator — designate a security account to administer GuardDuty/Security Hub organization-wide
Creating IAM users in each account
Sharing the management account credentials
VPC peering
explain: A delegated administrator account centrally manages GuardDuty and Security Hub across the organization, keeping daily security operations out of the management account. Per-account IAM users don't centralize anything, sharing management credentials violates every security practice, and VPC peering is network connectivity unrelated to security administration.

q: A company replicates encrypted EBS snapshots to a second Region for DR. The KMS key exists only in the primary Region, complicating decryption during failover. Which key type simplifies cross-region encrypted DR?
options: AWS-managed keys
KMS multi-Region keys — same key material replicated across Regions for encrypt/decrypt in either
SSE-S3 keys
Disabling encryption for DR copies
explain: Multi-Region keys replicate the same key material to secondary Regions, so data encrypted in one Region decrypts in another without re-encryption workflows. AWS-managed keys are region-scoped without multi-Region support, SSE-S3 keys only apply to S3 objects, and dropping encryption on DR copies weakens the security posture.

q: A deployment pipeline publishes Lambda functions. The security team wants AWS to verify that only approved, untampered code packages can be deployed — blocking anything not signed by the build system. Which service provides code signing validation for Lambda?
options: IAM policies on the deploy role
S3 versioning of deployment packages
AWS Signer — signs code packages and Lambda validates signatures at deploy time
CloudTrail
explain: AWS Signer creates trusted signatures during the build, and Lambda's code-signing configuration rejects any package that isn't validly signed. IAM policies control who can deploy rather than the integrity of what's deployed, versioning aids recovery rather than validation, and CloudTrail only records that an unsigned deployment happened.

q: A B2B API on API Gateway must authenticate calling systems using client certificates issued by the partner's CA — no API keys or tokens. Which API Gateway feature validates client certificates during the TLS handshake?
options: Lambda authorizers
API keys with usage plans
Cognito user pools
Mutual TLS (mTLS) — API Gateway validates the client certificate against a trusted CA bundle
explain: Mutual TLS terminates the handshake only when the client presents a certificate chaining to the configured truststore, authenticating systems without shared secrets. Lambda authorizers validate tokens rather than handshake certificates, API keys are shared secrets rather than certificates, and Cognito user pools authenticate human users rather than B2B systems.

q: A Cognito user pool faces password-spraying attacks with breached credentials. The team wants adaptive risk scoring, compromised-credential detection, and automatic response (like requiring MFA) without building it themselves. Which Cognito feature provides this?
options: Advanced Security Mode — compromised credential checks, adaptive authentication, and risk-based MFA
Standard user pool with MFA always on
IAM password policy
WAF rate-based rules alone
explain: Advanced Security Mode checks logins against compromised-credential databases and applies risk-based adaptive authentication, stepping up to MFA only for risky sign-ins. Always-on MFA adds friction for every user without detecting breached passwords, IAM password policies govern AWS operators rather than app users, and WAF rate rules act at the network level without credential intelligence.

q: Multiple accounts upload objects to a central logging bucket, and ACLs keep causing ownership confusion — the bucket owner can't read some objects. The team wants to disable ACLs entirely so the bucket owner owns everything. Which setting does this?
options: Bucket policies alone
S3 Object Ownership set to BucketOwnerEnforced — ACLs are disabled and the bucket owner owns all objects
Block Public Access
Versioning
explain: BucketOwnerEnforced disables all ACLs so every object is owned by the bucket owner regardless of which account wrote it. Bucket policies alone don't disable ACLs, Block Public Access governs public exposure rather than object ownership, and versioning preserves object versions without changing ownership.

q: Hundreds of EC2 instances mount an EFS file system, but each application team should only access its own directory with its own POSIX permissions. Managing per-instance mount options is unmanageable. Which EFS feature provides per-application access control?
options: EBS volumes per team
A single security group
EFS access points with IAM authorization — per-application mount points enforcing user, group, and directory
S3 bucket policies
explain: Access points give each application its own mount target with enforced POSIX user, group, and root directory, plus IAM authorization on top. Per-team EBS volumes abandon the shared file system, a security group filters network traffic rather than file access, and S3 bucket policies apply to a different service.

q: A company runs steady EC2 workloads on the same instance family in one Region for 3 years. They want the deepest possible discount and don't need to change families. Which commitment offers the highest discount for this fixed pattern?
options: On-Demand
Spot Instances
Compute Savings Plans
EC2 Instance Savings Plans — commit to an instance family and Region for the deepest EC2 discount
explain: EC2 Instance Savings Plans trade flexibility for the steepest discount, rewarding the commitment to a specific instance family and Region. On-Demand has no discount, Spot offers no price certainty for steady workloads, and Compute Savings Plans are more flexible but discount less deeply.

q: A company buys Reserved Instances for a critical workload that must be able to launch in a specific AZ even during capacity shortages. Which RI scope includes a capacity reservation?
options: Zonal Reserved Instances — reserve capacity in a specific AZ
Regional Reserved Instances
Compute Savings Plans
Spot Instances
explain: Zonal RIs reserve actual capacity in the chosen AZ, guaranteeing launchability during shortages. Regional RIs and Savings Plans are billing constructs that discount usage without reserving capacity, and Spot provides no guarantees at all.

q: A batch workload needs a guaranteed base of 20 instances plus up to 80 more when cheap capacity is available. The team wants cost savings without risking the base capacity. Which Auto Scaling configuration meets this?
options: 100% Spot Instances
Mixed instances policy with On-Demand base capacity and Spot overflow — guaranteed base, discounted burst
100% On-Demand
Manual instance launches
explain: A mixed instances policy pins the base capacity to On-Demand while bursting onto Spot, combining guaranteed availability with discounted scale. All-Spot risks losing the base to interruptions, all-On-Demand forfeits the Spot savings, and manual launches add toil without automation.

q: A team sets a lifecycle rule transitioning 50 million 4 KB objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 30 days, expecting big savings. The bill barely changes. Which S3 pricing detail explains this?
options: Transitions are free
Glacier retrieval is free
Small objects have a 128 KB minimum billable size and transitions cost per request — millions of tiny objects incur minimum-size charges and transition fees that erase the savings
Lifecycle rules don't apply to small objects
explain: Each tiny object is billed as 128 KB in archive tiers and every transition is a billed request, so 50 million small objects rack up minimum-size and request charges that swamp the per-GB savings. Transitions are billed per 1,000 requests, retrievals are billed, and lifecycle rules do apply to small objects — just uneconomically.

q: A bucket holds 100 million tiny objects with unpredictable access. Intelligent-Tiering seems ideal, but the team is warned it may not save money here. Why?
options: Intelligent-Tiering doesn't support small objects
It only works with versioning
It requires manual tier moves
The per-object monitoring and automation fee applies to every object — for 100 million tiny objects the fee can exceed the tiering savings
explain: Intelligent-Tiering charges a small monthly monitoring fee per object; multiplied by 100 million tiny objects, that fee alone can outweigh the storage-tier savings. The class supports small objects, works with or without versioning, and moves objects between tiers automatically.

q: A team moves objects to S3 Standard-IA and deletes many of them after 10 days. They expect 10 days of IA charges but are billed for more. Why?
options: Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum storage charge — early deletions are billed for the remaining days
IA charges a retrieval fee on delete
Deletes are billed as PUTs
Lifecycle rules override minimums
explain: Standard-IA bills a 30-day minimum per object, so deleting at day 10 still incurs the remaining 20 days. There is no retrieval fee on deletes, deletes aren't billed as PUTs, and lifecycle rules don't waive the minimum-duration charge.

q: Quarterly reports are archived to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and deleted after 45 days. The archive bill is higher than expected. What explains this?
options: Glacier charges per download only
Glacier Flexible Retrieval has a 90-day minimum storage charge — deleting at 45 days still bills the remaining 45
Archives can't be deleted
Cross-region replication is mandatory
explain: Glacier Flexible Retrieval carries a 90-day minimum storage charge per archive, so early deletion bills the prorated remainder. Billing covers storage duration rather than downloads alone, archives can be deleted (with the minimum applying), and replication is optional.

q: An application serves 100 TB/month of downloads directly from S3 in us-east-1 to global users. Data transfer costs dominate the bill. Which change typically reduces per-GB transfer costs for global downloads?
options: S3 Transfer Acceleration
Cross-region replication
Serve downloads through CloudFront — CloudFront data transfer out pricing is lower than direct S3 regional egress, plus edge caching cuts origin fetches
Larger EC2 instances as download proxies
explain: CloudFront's data-transfer-out rates undercut direct S3 regional egress, and edge caching means repeated downloads never touch the origin at all. Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads while adding charges, replication multiplies storage without cutting egress, and proxy instances add compute cost on top of the same transfer.

q: A development VPC spans three AZs with one NAT gateway per AZ. NAT gateway hourly charges are significant for an environment used 8 hours a day. Which change cuts NAT costs with an accepted resilience tradeoff for dev?
options: Add a fourth NAT gateway
Move dev workloads to public subnets
Route all traffic through an internet gateway from private subnets
Consolidate to a single NAT gateway — one hourly charge instead of three, accepting the AZ-level single point of failure for non-production
explain: One NAT gateway pays one hourly charge instead of three, a reasonable tradeoff for dev where an AZ failure is tolerable. More gateways increase cost, public subnets expose dev workloads, and private subnets can't route outbound traffic through an internet gateway directly.

q: Development RDS instances run 24/7 but are used only during business hours. Which approach eliminates compute charges nights and weekends?
options: Stop the RDS instances nights and weekends — stopped instances incur no compute charges (up to 7 days per stop)
Delete the instances nightly and restore from snapshot each morning
Switch to Multi-AZ
Buy Reserved Instances
explain: Stopping an RDS instance halts compute billing while preserving the data, and automation can stop/start on schedule. Nightly delete-and-restore is slow and toil-heavy, Multi-AZ doubles instance cost, and Reserved Instances commit to the 24/7 pattern instead of eliminating idle hours.

q: A production RDS database runs 24/7 at steady utilization and will for the next 3 years. The instance family is stable. Which purchase lowers the database cost the most?
options: On-Demand with auto scaling storage
RDS Reserved Instances for a 3-year term — deep discount for the steady commitment
Aurora Serverless v1
Read replicas instead of the primary
explain: A 3-year RDS Reserved Instance matches the steady, unchanging workload with the deepest commitment discount. On-Demand has no discount, Serverless v1's pause-to-zero pricing suits sporadic use rather than 24/7 steady load, and read replicas can't replace the primary's write role.

q: An Aurora cluster is used for testing a few hours per day. The team wants zero compute charges when idle but needs the data preserved. Which option fits?
options: Delete the cluster when idle
Aurora Serverless v2
Stop the Aurora cluster — compute billing stops and the cluster can be restarted within 7 days
Reduce to the smallest instance permanently
explain: Stopping the cluster halts compute charges while keeping all data intact for restart within 7 days. Deleting risks data loss and adds snapshot toil, Serverless v2 scales down to a 0.5 ACU minimum rather than zero, and the smallest provisioned instance still bills around the clock.

q: A DynamoDB table stores 2 TB of data accessed a few times per month, with occasional bursts. Standard table class storage costs are high for rarely-read data. Which table class lowers storage cost for infrequent access?
options: On-demand capacity mode
DAX
Global tables
DynamoDB Standard-IA table class — lower storage cost for infrequently accessed data with the same performance
explain: The Standard-IA table class cuts storage costs for data accessed infrequently while keeping the same latency and throughput. On-demand mode changes throughput pricing rather than storage class, DAX is a caching layer that doesn't alter storage pricing, and global tables add replication cost.

q: A Lambda function runs millions of invocations per month at 1024 MB, chosen by guesswork. The team suspects a different memory size would be cheaper overall. Which tool finds the most cost-efficient memory setting empirically?
options: AWS Lambda Power Tuning — runs the function at multiple memory sizes and compares cost vs duration
Increasing timeout
Provisioned concurrency
X-Ray tracing
explain: Power Tuning executes the function across memory configurations and charts the cost-duration tradeoff, replacing guesswork with data. Timeout only caps execution, provisioned concurrency addresses cold starts while adding cost, and X-Ray provides observability rather than cost optimization.

q: A high-traffic Lambda function logs verbosely and CloudWatch Logs ingestion plus 1-year retention is now a top-10 cost line. Which change cuts log costs while keeping a year of searchable history?
options: Disable all logging
Shorten the log group retention and export logs to S3 with a lifecycle policy to Glacier — cheap long-term storage
Increase retention to never expire
More detailed monitoring
explain: Short retention in CloudWatch Logs plus export to S3 with Glacier lifecycle keeps a year of history at archive prices instead of log-service prices. Disabling logging blinds operations, never-expire retention maximizes cost, and detailed monitoring adds metric charges.

q: Compliance requires keeping EBS snapshots for 7 years, but snapshots older than 90 days are almost never restored. Standard snapshot storage for 7 years is expensive. Which tier lowers the cost of long-term snapshot retention?
options: Delete snapshots after 90 days
Copy snapshots to more Regions
EBS Snapshot Archive tier — low-cost long-term snapshot storage with 24-72 hour restore
Keep snapshots on the source volumes
explain: The Archive tier stores rarely-restored snapshots at a fraction of standard snapshot pricing, with full restore available within 24-72 hours. Deleting violates the 7-year requirement, more regional copies multiply cost, and snapshots can't live on their source volumes — they're stored in S3-backed storage.

q: An EFS file system holds 10 TB, but 80% hasn't been touched in months. The team pays Standard rates for all of it. Which feature automatically moves idle files to cheaper storage?
options: EFS One Zone
Provisioned throughput
EBS snapshots of the mount targets
EFS lifecycle management — transitions files untouched for N days to the Infrequent Access storage class
explain: Lifecycle management automatically tiers files idle for the configured days to Infrequent Access pricing with no application changes. One Zone changes AZ scope rather than tiering by access, provisioned throughput is a performance setting, and EBS snapshots don't apply to EFS file systems.

q: A dev team needs a shared POSIX file system for build artifacts that are easily regenerated. Multi-AZ resilience isn't required. Which EFS storage class is cheapest for this reproducible data?
options: EFS One Zone and EFS One Zone-IA — single-AZ storage at lower cost for non-critical data
EFS Standard
FSx for Lustre
EBS io2 Multi-Attach
explain: One Zone classes store data in a single AZ at a lower price, which fits reproducible build artifacts that don't need AZ-level resilience. Standard charges for multi-AZ durability the workload doesn't need, FSx for Lustre is premium HPC performance, and io2 Multi-Attach is block storage rather than a shared POSIX file system.

q: A low-traffic internal web app averages 8% CPU with occasional spikes to 70%. The team runs it on an M6i.large at low utilization. Which instance choice fits this spiky, low-average pattern at lower cost?
options: A larger M instance
Burstable T instances (e.g., T3) — baseline CPU with burst credits for spikes, at a lower hourly rate
Compute-optimized C instances
Dedicated Hosts
explain: Burstable instances accrue CPU credits during idle periods and spend them on spikes, matching the 8%-average/70%-peak pattern at a lower rate than general-purpose instances. A larger M instance deepens the waste, C instances suit sustained high CPU, and Dedicated Hosts are premium-priced for licensing scenarios.

q: Containerized services on Fargate run 24/7 at steady utilization. The team is told Fargate's per-second pricing may not be cheapest for always-on workloads. Which alternative typically lowers cost for sustained container workloads?
options: Lambda
Fargate Spot for everything
ECS on EC2 launch type — pay for the instances, which is typically cheaper than Fargate for sustained utilization
Larger Fargate task sizes
explain: For steady 24/7 utilization, EC2 instances under ECS usually beat Fargate's per-vCPU-hour premium since the capacity is fully used. Lambda's per-invocation pricing suits sporadic work rather than always-on services, Fargate Spot risks interruptions for steady workloads, and larger tasks just consume more of the premium-priced capacity.

q: An ECR repository accumulates thousands of old container images from every CI build. Storage costs grow monthly. Which feature automatically removes old images?
options: Manual console deletes
S3 lifecycle policies
ECR replication
ECR lifecycle policies — expire images by count or age automatically
explain: ECR lifecycle policies automatically expire untagged or aging images by rule, stopping the storage growth with no toil. Manual deletes don't scale with CI volume, S3 lifecycle policies don't apply to ECR, and replication copies images to other Regions, increasing cost.

q: A Redshift cluster is used for analytics only during business hours. Compute charges accrue 24/7. Which feature stops compute billing nights and weekends?
options: Pause and resume — paused clusters incur no compute charges, only managed storage
Delete the cluster nightly
Concurrency scaling always on
Single-node cluster
explain: Pausing stops compute billing while the data remains in managed storage, and resume brings the cluster back for business hours. Nightly deletion adds snapshot-restore toil and risk, always-on concurrency scaling adds burst charges, and a single-node cluster still bills 24/7.

q: A nightly Spark ETL job runs on a long-running EMR cluster that sits idle 20 hours a day. Which design runs the job at the lowest cost?
options: A bigger long-running cluster
Transient EMR cluster launched per job with Spot task nodes — cluster exists only during the run, task nodes at Spot discounts
On-Demand core nodes 24/7
Manual cluster management
explain: A transient cluster eliminates the 20 idle hours entirely, and Spot task nodes discount the compute during the run. A bigger cluster deepens the idle waste, 24/7 On-Demand core nodes are the current expensive pattern, and manual management adds toil without cutting the idle hours.

q: A team streams application logs to S3 for archival. They use Kinesis Data Streams with provisioned shards but do no real-time stream processing — consumers just batch-load to S3. Which service delivers the same outcome at lower cost and less management?
options: More shards
MSK
Kinesis Data Firehose — fully managed delivery to S3 with no shards to manage, priced per GB ingested
SQS FIFO
explain: Firehose buffers and delivers records to S3 automatically with no shards to provision or monitor, and per-GB pricing beats paying for idle shard hours. More shards increase the waste, MSK is a heavier Kafka service for streaming workloads that need it, and SQS FIFO is a queue without built-in S3 delivery.

q: A team invalidates their entire CloudFront distribution (/*) on every deployment — dozens of times per day — and invalidation charges are climbing. Which practice eliminates most invalidation costs?
options: More frequent invalidations
Longer TTLs with no versioning
Disabling CloudFront caching
Versioned filenames (e.g., app.v2.js) — new deployments use new URLs, so no invalidation is needed
explain: Versioned filenames make each deployment a new cache object, so there's nothing stale to invalidate — only the first 1,000 invalidation paths per month are free, after which each path is billed. More invalidations multiply the charge, long TTLs without versioning serve stale content, and disabling caching forfeits edge performance.

q: A checkout service depends on three components: the web tier, the payment API, and the inventory database. The team wants Route 53 to fail over to a standby Region only when all three components are unhealthy — not when a single component has a brief blip. Which Route 53 feature combines the individual health checks into one overall verdict?
options: Create one health check per component and page on-call for each
A CloudWatch composite alarm on the three metrics
A calculated health check that combines the three health checks with AND/OR/NOT logic
Latency-based routing between the Regions
explain: Calculated health checks aggregate multiple health checks using boolean logic, so failover triggers only when the combined condition (e.g., all three unhealthy) holds. Per-component checks page on partial blips, CloudWatch composite alarms combine alarms rather than Route 53 health checks, and latency-based routing steers by latency without any health aggregation.

q: A Network Load Balancer spans three AZs, but nearly all registered targets ended up in one AZ, which is now overloaded while the other AZs sit idle. The team assumed traffic would spread evenly because 'that's what load balancers do.' What is the fix?
options: Enable cross-zone load balancing on the NLB — unlike ALB, it is disabled by default on NLB
Register more targets in the overloaded AZ
Replace the NLB with an ALB
Enable sticky sessions on the target group
explain: Cross-zone load balancing is on by default for ALB but off by default for NLB, so each NLB AZ node was sending traffic only to its local targets. Enabling it spreads traffic across all targets. Adding targets to the overloaded AZ worsens the imbalance, swapping to ALB loses NLB's static IPs and TCP performance, and sticky sessions pin clients without rebalancing.

q: A producer retries failed sends to an SQS FIFO queue, and the retries occasionally create duplicate messages that corrupt downstream accounting. The producer cannot reliably track message IDs across restarts. Which FIFO feature deduplicates automatically?
options: Switch to a standard queue with best-effort ordering
Increase the visibility timeout
Use larger batch sizes
Enable content-based deduplication — SQS uses the SHA-256 hash of the message body as the deduplication ID
explain: Content-based deduplication hashes the message body so identical retries within the 5-minute deduplication window are automatically dropped, with no ID tracking needed. A standard queue abandons ordering and still allows duplicates, visibility timeout governs consumer redelivery timing rather than producer duplicates, and batch size doesn't deduplicate.

q: A Lambda function polls an SQS queue. One malformed 'poison' message fails every processing attempt, gets retried indefinitely, and blocks the rest of the batch behind it. Which configuration isolates the poison message while letting good messages flow?
options: Increase the batch size so the poison message is diluted
Set a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount on the source queue so repeatedly failing messages move to a dead-letter queue for inspection, combined with partial batch responses
Delete the dead-letter queue to force retries
Increase the Lambda timeout
explain: maxReceiveCount moves a message to the DLQ after N failed receives, removing the poison message from the main flow for later inspection, while partial batch responses keep good messages from being reprocessed. A larger batch still retries the poison message, deleting the DLQ removes the isolation mechanism, and a longer timeout doesn't fix a message that can never succeed.

q: A company runs RDS for PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ instance deployment, but failover still takes too long for its SLA and the standby cannot serve read traffic. Which RDS deployment gives faster failover plus readable standbys?
options: An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster — two readable standby instances with automated failover typically under 35 seconds
Adding cross-region read replicas
Switching to a Single-AZ deployment with larger storage
Enabling storage autoscaling
explain: A Multi-AZ DB cluster keeps two readable standbys and fails over in typically under 35 seconds, versus the single non-readable standby and slower failover of a Multi-AZ instance deployment. Read replicas are asynchronous and need manual promotion, Single-AZ removes failover entirely, and storage autoscaling addresses capacity rather than failover speed.

q: A fleet processes long-running video encodes on EC2 in an Auto Scaling group. During scale-in, instances running active encodes are terminated mid-job and customers lose their renders. The team wants the simplest control that stops scale-in from killing busy instances. Which should they use?
options: Disable the Auto Scaling group entirely
Move the encodes to Spot Instances
Enable instance scale-in protection on instances with active jobs (cleared by the application when the encode finishes)
Increase the cooldown period
explain: Scale-in protection tells Auto Scaling not to terminate specific instances during scale-in, and the application clears it when the job completes — the simplest guard for long-running work. Disabling the group removes all scaling, Spot makes interruptions more likely, and the cooldown period paces scaling actions rather than protecting busy instances.

q: A clustered database running on EC2 needs shared block storage visible to multiple instances simultaneously within one AZ, with high IOPS. EFS and FSx don't fit because the cluster needs raw block devices. Which EBS feature provides this?
options: EBS gp3 volumes shared via NFS
Instance store volumes
EBS snapshots
EBS Multi-Attach on io1/io2 volumes — attach one volume to up to 16 Nitro-based instances in the same AZ
explain: Multi-Attach lets multiple instances in the same AZ share a single io1/io2 volume, which is exactly what clustered applications needing concurrent block access require. gp3 doesn't support Multi-Attach, instance store is ephemeral and per-instance, and snapshots are point-in-time backups rather than live shared storage.

q: A travel booking flow reserves a flight, charges the card, then books the hotel. If the hotel booking fails, the flight reservation and the charge must be undone. There is no distributed transaction coordinator across these services. Which pattern handles this correctly?
options: Two-phase commit across the three services
A single Lambda function with a long timeout
SQS FIFO ordering guarantees
The saga pattern in Step Functions — each step has a compensating transaction that undoes it if a later step fails
explain: The saga pattern sequences local transactions with compensating actions (cancel flight, refund charge) that run when a downstream step fails, giving transactional semantics without a distributed coordinator. Two-phase commit isn't available across independent services, one giant Lambda can't span the failure windows reliably, and FIFO ordering guarantees sequence rather than atomicity.

q: A company is migrating its RabbitMQ workloads to AWS and needs both high availability across AZs and horizontal scalability as queue depth grows. Which Amazon MQ deployment meets both needs?
options: Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ with the cluster deployment mode — multiple brokers across AZs for scale and failover
A single-instance Amazon MQ broker
Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ in active/standby mode
Amazon SQS standard queues
explain: The RabbitMQ cluster deployment mode runs multiple brokers across AZs, scaling throughput horizontally while surviving broker or AZ failures. A single-instance broker is a single point of failure, ActiveMQ active/standby gives HA without horizontal scaling (and is a different engine), and SQS would force a protocol rewrite away from AMQP.

q: A company runs Amazon MSK in us-east-1 and needs selected Kafka topics continuously replicated to eu-west-1 for disaster recovery, without operating MirrorMaker clusters on EC2. Which managed solution provides this?
options: MSK tiered storage
Increasing the topic retention period
MSK Replicator — managed cross-cluster replication built on MirrorMaker 2
Kinesis Data Streams
explain: MSK Replicator is the managed MirrorMaker 2 implementation that replicates topics across MSK clusters and Regions with no brokers to operate. Tiered storage extends retention within one cluster rather than replicating, longer retention doesn't copy data cross-region, and Kinesis is a different streaming service requiring an application rewrite.

q: A company connects branch offices to AWS with Site-to-Site VPN, but users complain about inconsistent throughput and high latency over the public internet. Dedicated Direct Connect to every branch is not feasible. Which option improves VPN performance using the AWS global network?
options: Larger VPN tunnel bandwidth settings
A second VPN tunnel over the same internet path
AWS Client VPN for the branches
An accelerated Site-to-Site VPN — routes VPN traffic through AWS Global Accelerator's edge network
explain: Accelerated VPN attaches the VPN connection to a Global Accelerator, so branch traffic enters the AWS edge network close to the user and rides the private backbone instead of the variable public internet. Bigger tunnel settings don't fix internet congestion, a second tunnel shares the same path, and Client VPN is for individual devices rather than branch sites.

q: A team runs an Aurora Global Database and needs to perform planned maintenance on the primary Region with zero data loss. An unplanned failover risks losing recent writes. Which approach should they use for the planned event?
options: Delete the secondary cluster and rebuild it after maintenance
A managed planned switchover — AWS orchestrates promoting the secondary with no data loss when the primary is healthy
An unplanned failover to the secondary Region
Restore from the latest snapshot in the secondary Region
explain: Managed switchover is designed for planned events: with a healthy primary it promotes the secondary without data loss and reverses replication cleanly. Unplanned failover is the DR path and can lose in-flight writes, deleting the secondary destroys the DR posture, and snapshot restore has an RPO back to the snapshot time.

q: Regulations require financial records in S3 to be immutable (WORM), but the compliance team must retain the ability to delete objects in rare, audited legal scenarios. Compliance mode is too strict for this. Which Object Lock mode fits?
options: Governance mode — objects are WORM-protected, but users with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can override
Compliance mode, which nobody including root can override
Versioning without Object Lock
MFA Delete
explain: Governance mode enforces WORM retention while still allowing specifically permissioned users to bypass it for legal holds or corrections. Compliance mode blocks everyone including root for the retention period, versioning alone doesn't prevent privileged deletion, and MFA Delete only guards version deletion rather than enforcing retention.

q: An application writes to the same DynamoDB item from us-east-1 and eu-west-1 nearly simultaneously using global tables. Both writes succeed. Which version of the item survives?
options: Both versions are merged field by field
The write fails with a conflict error
Last-writer-wins — the item with the latest timestamp prevails, so applications must design for idempotent, reconcilable writes
The us-east-1 write always wins as the original Region
explain: DynamoDB global tables resolve concurrent cross-region writes with last-writer-wins based on timestamps; there is no merge or conflict error. Applications must therefore make writes idempotent and tolerant of overwrites. Field-level merging doesn't happen, conflicts don't raise errors, and no Region has inherent priority.

q: A team rolls out new AMIs to an Auto Scaling group, but a bad AMI last quarter replaced every instance before the bug was caught. They want replacements to proceed in stages with a pause for validation between stages, aborting automatically on CloudWatch alarms. Which feature provides this?
options: Terminating all instances manually at once
Creating a second Auto Scaling group for each deploy
Suspending all scaling processes
Instance refresh with checkpoints and CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback
explain: Instance refresh replaces instances gradually, pauses at configured checkpoints for validation, and rolls back automatically when alarms breach — containing a bad AMI to a fraction of the fleet. Manual termination has no staging or rollback, a second group per deploy is heavyweight toil, and suspending scaling processes freezes the group rather than updating it safely.

q: A stateful web application stores sessions in instance memory and uses sticky sessions. Every Auto Scaling replacement event logs users out and drops shopping carts. Which change makes sessions survive instance replacement?
options: Longer sticky session durations
Externalize session state to DynamoDB (or ElastiCache) so any instance can serve any user after replacements
Larger EC2 instances with more RAM
Shorter Auto Scaling cooldowns
explain: External session storage decouples user state from instance lifecycle, so terminated instances take no sessions with them and no stickiness is needed. Longer stickiness still breaks on termination, bigger instances still get replaced, and cooldowns only pace scaling actions.

q: A company needs shared NFS and SMB file storage with point-in-time snapshots, cloning, and cross-region disaster recovery replication. The file system must survive an AZ failure automatically. Which solution meets all of these?
options: FSx for NetApp ONTAP with Multi-AZ deployment and SnapMirror replication to a second Region
Amazon EFS with replication
FSx for Windows File Server Single-AZ
EBS volumes with Multi-Attach
explain: FSx for ONTAP provides the NetApp feature set (snapshots, FlexClones, multiprotocol NFS/SMB), Multi-AZ deployment for automatic failover, and SnapMirror for cross-region replication. EFS lacks ONTAP snapshots, cloning, and SnapMirror; FSx for Windows is SMB-only without SnapMirror; and Multi-Attach EBS is block storage, not a managed file system.

q: A disaster recovery runbook restores 4 TB EBS volumes from snapshots, but the first access to each block is slow while data lazily loads from S3, blowing the RTO. Which feature pre-initializes snapshot blocks so restored volumes perform immediately?
options: Taking snapshots more frequently
Using larger volumes
EBS Fast Snapshot Restore — pre-warms snapshot data so volumes created from the snapshot are fully performant at creation
Enabling EBS encryption
explain: Fast Snapshot Restore eliminates lazy loading by pre-initializing all snapshot blocks, so restored volumes deliver full performance instantly, meeting tight RTOs. More frequent snapshots don't change restore laziness, larger volumes restore even more slowly, and encryption doesn't affect initialization speed.

q: An order pipeline fans out events to inventory, billing, and notification services, and every consumer must process each order exactly once and in the same sequence. Standard SNS fan-out can reorder and duplicate. Which design preserves order and exactly-once semantics across all consumers?
options: SNS standard topic with three SQS standard queues
EventBridge with three rules
Kinesis Data Streams with one shard per consumer
An SNS FIFO topic fanning out to SQS FIFO queues — FIFO semantics preserved end to end
explain: SNS FIFO to SQS FIFO subscriptions preserve message ordering and deduplication across the fan-out, so every consumer sees the same ordered, deduplicated stream. Standard SNS/SQS offer no ordering or dedup guarantees, EventBridge doesn't provide strict ordering, and per-consumer Kinesis shards multiply cost and complexity unnecessarily.

q: A lightweight API runs on EC2 instances in two AZs with no load balancer, and the team wants DNS to return only healthy instance IPs so clients can retry across them. Which Route 53 policy fits this simple active-active setup?
options: Geolocation routing
Multivalue answer routing — returns up to eight healthy records so clients can fail over between them
Failover routing
Weighted routing with 50/50 weights and no health checks
explain: Multivalue answer routing returns multiple healthy A records (up to eight) and excludes unhealthy ones via health checks, giving simple client-side failover without a load balancer. Geolocation routes by user location rather than health, failover routing is active-passive, and weighted records without health checks keep serving impaired endpoints.

q: A company runs production microservices on EKS. A node AZ impairment last month evicted too many pods at once and caused an outage. Which combination keeps the cluster resilient to node and AZ failures?
options: Managed node groups spread across multiple AZs, PodDisruptionBudgets limiting simultaneous evictions, and Cluster Autoscaler replacing failed nodes
A single node group in one AZ with large instances
Static self-managed nodes with no autoscaling
Running all pods on Fargate with no node groups
explain: Multi-AZ node groups distribute pods across failure domains, PodDisruptionBudgets cap how many pods can go down at once during disruptions, and Cluster Autoscaler restores capacity automatically. A single-AZ node group concentrates risk, static nodes can't self-heal, and Fargate alone doesn't address AZ distribution or eviction budgets for the workloads that need nodes.

q: A central security account runs an EventBridge event bus that must receive security findings from 40 member accounts. The member accounts' PutEvents calls are denied. What is missing?
options: VPC peering between the accounts
An SNS topic in each member account
A resource-based policy on the central event bus allowing events:PutEvents from the member accounts
IAM users in the central account for each member
explain: Cross-account EventBridge delivery requires a resource-based policy on the destination event bus granting PutEvents to the source accounts — identity policies alone can't authorize another account's bus. VPC peering is irrelevant to EventBridge, per-account SNS topics add unneeded hops, and IAM users per member account is credential sprawl.

q: A company runs RDS for MySQL (not Aurora) and needs a disaster recovery copy in a second Region with an RPO of minutes. On disaster, the secondary must become a standalone writable database quickly. Which approach meets this?
options: Multi-AZ deployment, which only protects within one Region
Nightly snapshot copies to the second Region
Enabling storage autoscaling
A cross-region read replica — asynchronous replication with minute-scale RPO, promoted to standalone on disaster
explain: Cross-region read replicas stream changes asynchronously for a minute-scale RPO and promote to a standalone writable instance during DR. Multi-AZ doesn't cross Regions, nightly snapshots give a 24-hour RPO, and storage autoscaling addresses capacity rather than disaster recovery.

q: A CloudWatch alarm monitors a sparse custom metric that only emits data during errors. The team wants the alarm to fire if the metric stops reporting entirely, which would indicate the emitter died. How should the alarm treat missing data?
options: Treat missing data as 'notBreaching' so the alarm stays quiet
Treat missing data as 'breaching' — silence from the emitter becomes an alarm condition
Lower the alarm threshold to zero
Increase the evaluation periods
explain: Treating missing data as breaching turns emitter silence into an alert, catching the dead-emitter scenario the team cares about. 'NotBreaching' would mask exactly this failure, a zero threshold doesn't fire when there's no data to evaluate, and more evaluation periods just delay the verdict.

q: After a ransomware incident at a peer company, a CTO wants backups that remain recoverable even if attackers compromise the AWS management account itself. Standard cross-region copies still live inside the organization's control plane. Which AWS Backup feature provides the strongest isolation?
options: Logically air-gapped vaults — backups stored in an AWS-managed vault outside the customer's control plane, optionally with Vault Lock
More frequent backups in the same account
S3 versioning on the backup bucket
Cross-account backup with the same organization
explain: Logically air-gapped vaults hold recovery points in AWS-managed storage outside the customer's accounts and control plane, so compromised management credentials can't reach them; Vault Lock adds immutability. Same-account or same-organization copies remain reachable by compromised credentials, and versioning doesn't isolate the control plane.

q: A team is designing an S3 key scheme with complex hash prefixes because they believe S3 still needs randomized prefixes for high request rates. What should they know about current S3 partition performance?
options: Randomized prefixes are still required for any serious workload
S3 now automatically scales to at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix — no prefix randomization needed
Prefixes are limited to 100 requests per second
Only CloudFront can raise S3 request rates
explain: S3 automatically partitions to sustain at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per prefix, so the old guidance to randomize prefixes for performance is obsolete. Randomized prefixes add complexity for no gain, there is no 100-request limit, and CloudFront caches content but doesn't change S3's per-prefix request scaling.

q: A DynamoDB table on provisioned capacity has one partition key value receiving 80% of all writes. That partition throttles while overall table utilization looks fine. The team must stay on provisioned mode for cost reasons. Which design change fixes the hot partition?
options: Add a global secondary index
Enable DynamoDB Streams
Add DAX in front of the table
Write sharding — append a random suffix (e.g., 1-N) to the partition key to spread writes across partitions
explain: Write sharding distributes the hot key's traffic across N partitions, eliminating the single-partition throttle at the source. A GSI adds an alternate access pattern without fixing the base table's hot key, Streams capture changes rather than spreading writes, and DAX caches reads rather than write throughput.

q: A DynamoDB table needs a global secondary index so users can look up orders by email address. The GSI is only used to find the order ID, after which the app reads the full item from the base table. How should the GSI projection be configured to minimize cost?
options: KEYS_ONLY projection — the GSI stores only the key attributes, keeping it small since full items are fetched from the base table
ALL projection with every attribute
INCLUDE projection with all non-key attributes
No projection — GSIs always store everything
explain: KEYS_ONLY keeps the index minimal because the access pattern only needs the keys to locate the item before reading the full record from the base table, minimizing GSI storage and write costs. ALL or INCLUDE-everything duplicates the table's data into the index, and projections are configurable — they don't default to everything.

q: A team puts DAX in front of DynamoDB expecting it to speed up both reads and writes for a write-heavy leaderboard. Write latency doesn't improve. What should they understand about DAX?
options: DAX requires provisioned mode to accelerate writes
DAX only works with global tables
DAX is a write-through read cache — writes still go directly to DynamoDB, so it accelerates read-heavy workloads, not write-heavy ones
DAX must be placed in the same AZ as the table
explain: DAX caches item and query results for microsecond reads and writes through to DynamoDB, so write latency is unchanged — it's the wrong tool for a write-heavy workload. It works with both capacity modes, doesn't require global tables, and AZ placement isn't the issue; the workload pattern is.

q: An RDS for MySQL workload is read-heavy with a working set larger than RAM, and the team wants lower read latency without adding read replicas or changing the application. Which RDS feature uses local NVMe SSDs to accelerate reads?
options: Increasing the gp3 volume size
RDS Optimized Reads — instances with local NVMe SSDs cache data for faster reads
Enabling Multi-AZ
RDS Proxy
explain: RDS Optimized Reads places the database on instances with local NVMe SSD storage used as a fast cache tier, cutting read latency with no application changes. A bigger gp3 volume adds capacity rather than a faster cache tier, Multi-AZ addresses failover, and RDS Proxy pools connections rather than accelerating storage reads.

q: Analysts need to join 3 TB of historical clickstream data in S3 with live dimension tables in Redshift. Loading all 3 TB into the cluster for occasional queries is wasteful. Which feature queries the S3 data in place?
options: COPY the 3 TB into the cluster before every query
Concurrency scaling
Export the dimension tables to S3 and use Athena
Redshift Spectrum — query S3 data directly and join it with warehouse tables
explain: Redshift Spectrum lets the cluster query S3 data in place and join it with local tables, avoiding the load of 3 TB for occasional analysis. COPYing before every query is slow and wasteful, concurrency scaling adds burst compute rather than S3 access, and exporting dimensions to Athena inverts the architecture instead of joining in Redshift.

q: A Redshift cluster runs nightly ETL jobs and daytime analyst dashboards. The ETL's heavy loads starve dashboards of concurrency every morning. Which feature isolates the two workloads on the same cluster?
options: Workload Management (WLM) queues — separate queues with dedicated concurrency and memory for ETL vs dashboards
Taking hourly snapshots
Enabling result caching
Adding more disk storage
explain: WLM queues partition the cluster's concurrency and memory between workload classes, so ETL can't starve dashboards. Snapshots are for recovery, result caching helps repeated identical queries rather than concurrency isolation, and disk storage doesn't add query slots.

q: A data science team runs Spark jobs a few times per week with wildly varying sizes. Managing EMR clusters, instance types, and scaling for these sporadic jobs is pure overhead. Which option runs Spark with no cluster to manage?
options: A long-running EMR cluster sized for the largest job
EMR on EC2 with managed scaling
EMR Serverless — submit Spark jobs without provisioning or managing clusters
AWS Batch with single-node jobs
explain: EMR Serverless runs Spark (and Hive) jobs on managed capacity with automatic scaling and per-job billing — no clusters, instance types, or scaling policies. A long-running cluster idles between the weekly jobs, managed scaling still requires a cluster, and single-node Batch jobs don't run distributed Spark.

q: A Glue ETL job reloads the entire 2 TB source dataset every night even though only the day's new partition changed, wasting DPUs and time. Which feature makes the job process only new data?
options: Increasing the DPU count
Glue job bookmarks — track processed data so the job incrementally processes only new partitions
Running the job more frequently
Glue DataBrew
explain: Job bookmarks persist the state of processed data, so each run processes only new or changed partitions instead of the full 2 TB. More DPUs just parallelize the wasteful full reload, running more often multiplies the waste, and DataBrew is a visual data-prep tool rather than incremental state tracking.

q: A fraud-detection pipeline needs stateful stream processing: 10-minute session windows over click events with exactly-once aggregation, which per-record Lambda functions can't express. Which managed service provides this?
options: Kinesis Data Firehose
Lambda with larger batches
SQS FIFO queues
Managed Service for Apache Flink — stateful streaming with event-time windows and exactly-once semantics
explain: Managed Service for Apache Flink (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics) provides stateful operators, session/tumbling windows, and checkpointed exactly-once processing that per-record Lambda can't do. Firehose only delivers batches to destinations, bigger Lambda batches don't add windowing state, and SQS FIFO gives ordering without stream windows.

q: An MSK cluster must retain 90 days of Kafka topics for audit replay, but keeping 90 days on broker EBS volumes is expensive and forces larger brokers. Which feature offloads older topic data cheaply while keeping it consumable?
options: MSK tiered storage — transparently tiers older log segments to S3 while consumers still read them
Shortening retention to 7 days
Adding more broker nodes
Mirroring topics to a second cluster
explain: Tiered storage moves older segments to S3-backed storage that consumers read transparently, decoupling retention cost from broker sizing. Shorter retention violates the audit requirement, more brokers scale the expensive pattern, and a second cluster doubles infrastructure without tiering.

q: A Lambda function needs a 4 GB reference dataset on every invocation. Downloading it from S3 each time adds seconds of latency, and the 512 MB /tmp limit can't hold it. Which approach gives the function fast shared access to the dataset?
options: Packaging the dataset in the deployment package
Increasing function memory to 10 GB
Mounting an EFS file system on the function — shared, elastic storage accessible across invocations
Lambda SnapStart
explain: Lambda's EFS integration mounts a shared file system into the execution environment, so the 4 GB dataset is read directly without per-invocation downloads or /tmp limits. Deployment packages cap at 250 MB unzipped, memory doesn't expand /tmp, and SnapStart reduces cold starts without adding shared storage.

q: A Lambda function generates 15 MB PDF reports, but the buffered invoke response limit is 6 MB, forcing an awkward S3 write-then-redirect dance. Which feature streams large responses directly to the caller?
options: Increasing the function timeout
Lambda response streaming — stream payloads larger than the 6 MB buffered limit directly to clients
Provisioned concurrency
Splitting the PDF into 6 MB chunks in the client
explain: Response streaming sends the payload as it's produced, bypassing the 6 MB buffered invoke limit for large responses. Timeout caps duration rather than raising payload limits, provisioned concurrency addresses cold starts, and client-side chunking pushes complexity to every caller.

q: A team is building a collaborative whiteboard needing low-latency bidirectional messaging between browsers and the backend. Polling a REST API every second is laggy and expensive. Which API Gateway API type fits?
options: REST API with aggressive caching
HTTP API with JWT authorizers
Private REST API
WebSocket API — persistent bidirectional connections for real-time messaging
explain: WebSocket APIs maintain persistent connections with bidirectional message flow, purpose-built for real-time collaboration without polling. REST and HTTP APIs are request/response regardless of caching, and private APIs address network isolation rather than real-time messaging.

q: A team wants to canary a new version of their EC2-backed service: 10% of traffic to the new version, 90% to the old, behind a single ALB with instant rollback by shifting weights. Which ALB feature enables this?
options: Weighted target groups — forward rules split traffic by weight between the old and new target groups
