Two ALBs with Route 53 weighted records
Sticky sessions
Path-based routing only
explain: Weighted target groups let one ALB listener split traffic 90/10 between target groups and shift weights instantly for rollback. Two ALBs with DNS weighting works but adds a load balancer and DNS caching delays, sticky sessions pin users rather than splitting proportionally, and path-based routing splits by URL rather than by percentage.

q: An ECS service had all its tasks land on the same EC2 instance, and that instance's failure took the service down. The team wants tasks spread across instances and AZs for resilience. Which task placement strategy should they use?
options: Binpack — packs tasks tightly to minimize instance count
Daemon scheduling
Spread — distributes tasks evenly across AZs and instances
Random placement
explain: The spread strategy places tasks across availability zones and then across instances, so no single instance or AZ failure takes the whole service down. Binpack optimizes for cost by consolidating (the failure mode they just hit), daemon runs one task per instance for agents rather than services, and random gives no guarantees.

q: A company runs Cassandra across EC2 and needs rack awareness: nodes grouped so a rack-level failure takes down at most one replica set, with the placement topology visible to the application. Which placement group fits large distributed systems like this?
options: Cluster placement group
Partition placement group — spreads instances across logical partitions with no shared racks, topology-aware for HDFS, Cassandra, and Kafka
Spread placement group
No placement group
explain: Partition placement groups divide instances across partitions (up to 7 per AZ) with distinct racks per partition and expose the topology, which is exactly what rack-aware systems like Cassandra need. Cluster placement packs instances together for latency (the opposite), spread placement suits small fleets with one instance per rack, and no placement group gives no guarantees.

q: A database volume is running out of space during business hours. The team believes they must stop the instance, snapshot, and create a larger volume — causing downtime. What is the faster approach?
options: Add a second volume and use RAID
Migrate to instance store
Take a snapshot and wait
Modify the volume with EBS elastic volumes — increase size or change type live without detachment or downtime
explain: Elastic volumes allow live modification of size, IOPS, and type while the volume stays attached and the instance keeps running. RAID adds complexity without solving the resize, instance store is ephemeral, and snapshot-restore is the slow downtime path elastic volumes replace.

q: A multiplayer game backend on EC2 needs deterministic port mapping so each player's UDP traffic always lands on the same game server, with fixed global entry IPs. Standard Global Accelerator load balancing doesn't preserve the mapping. Which accelerator type provides this?
options: Custom routing accelerators — deterministic port-to-endpoint mapping for gaming and VoIP-style workloads
Standard accelerators with ALB endpoints
Route 53 latency-based routing
CloudFront
explain: Custom routing accelerators map listener port ranges deterministically to specific EC2 endpoints, preserving the player-to-server affinity the game needs. Standard accelerators distribute by health and proximity without deterministic mapping, Route 53 is DNS-based without port control, and CloudFront serves HTTP rather than UDP game traffic.

q: A Linux analytics team needs shared NFS storage with instant point-in-time snapshots and writable clones for testing, plus per-share throughput control. EFS doesn't offer clones. Which service provides ZFS-based file storage?
options: Amazon EFS
FSx for Lustre
FSx for OpenZFS — managed ZFS with snapshots, clones, and NFS for Linux workloads
S3 with File Gateway
explain: FSx for OpenZFS brings ZFS semantics — instant snapshots, writable clones, and dataset-level quotas — to managed NFS storage. EFS has no clone concept, FSx for Lustre targets HPC scratch throughput rather than ZFS data management, and File Gateway presents S3 as a file share without ZFS features.

q: A branch office needs its on-premises applications to read and write S3 objects through standard NFS and SMB mounts, with frequently accessed files cached locally for performance. Which service presents S3 as on-premises file shares?
options: AWS DataSync
S3 File Gateway — NFS/SMB shares backed by S3 with a local cache
FSx for Windows File Server
EBS volumes over VPN
explain: S3 File Gateway exposes S3 buckets as NFS/SMB mounts with a local cache for hot files, bridging on-premises apps to S3. DataSync is for migration/sync rather than persistent mounts, FSx for Windows isn't S3-backed, and EBS can't be shared over VPN as a file share.

q: A company must migrate 500 TB from an on-premises NAS to S3 over a 10 Gbps Direct Connect within a tight window, with checksum validation and incremental sync of changes made during the migration. Which service is purpose-built for this?
options: rsync over the VPN
S3 multipart upload from a script
AWS Snowball Edge for an online transfer
AWS DataSync — managed high-throughput transfer with scheduling, bandwidth controls, and data validation
explain: DataSync is engineered for large online migrations: parallelized transfers that saturate the link, incremental sync of deltas, and built-in integrity validation. rsync is single-threaded and slow at this scale, hand-rolled multipart scripts lack validation and scheduling, and Snowball Edge is the offline device for when the network can't carry the data.

q: A production OpenSearch cluster runs with all nodes in one AZ and data nodes doubling as cluster managers. An AZ impairment took the whole cluster down. Which design makes the domain resilient?
options: Zone awareness across three AZs with dedicated master nodes — cluster management separated from data nodes and spread across zones
Bigger data nodes in the same AZ
More replicas within the single AZ
Daily snapshots
explain: Zone awareness replicates shards across three AZs while dedicated master nodes keep cluster coordination stable and separate from data load, surviving an AZ loss. Bigger nodes in one AZ share the same failure domain, same-AZ replicas don't survive AZ impairment, and snapshots recover data but not availability.

q: An Elastic Beanstalk application had a bad deployment take the whole environment down because new code replaced all instances at once with no quick rollback. Which deployment policy launches the new version on fresh instances first and only terminates the old ones after health checks pass?
options: All at once
Rolling
Immutable — deploys to a new set of instances, shifts traffic after validation, and rolls back by keeping the old instances until success
Rolling with additional batch
explain: Immutable deployments provision a whole new instance set, validate health, then cut over — the old fleet stays intact for instant rollback. All-at-once causes full downtime on failure, rolling mixes versions with partial capacity risk, and rolling with additional batch still replaces in place rather than keeping a pristine fallback fleet.

q: An engineering simulation needs 32 tightly coupled nodes with MPI communication for a 6-hour run, orchestrated as one job with placement awareness. Single-node batch jobs can't express this. Which AWS Batch feature runs multi-node parallel workloads?
options: Array jobs
Multi-node parallel jobs — a single job spanning multiple EC2 instances with inter-node communication
Lambda functions
Fargate tasks
explain: Multi-node parallel jobs let one Batch job span coordinated EC2 instances with MPI-style communication, which is exactly the tightly coupled simulation pattern. Array jobs run many independent single-node jobs, Lambda can't do inter-node MPI, and Fargate tasks don't support multi-node parallel placement.

q: Engineers work on dozens of short-lived projects and need project-scoped access to S3 prefixes and DynamoDB tables. Creating a new IAM role per project is unsustainable. Which approach grants project-scoped permissions dynamically at sign-in?
options: One shared role with access to everything
Tagging resources with project names only
SCPs per project
Attribute-based access control (ABAC) — pass project as a session tag via sts:TagSession and write policies matching the principal's tag to the resource's tag
explain: ABAC with session tags lets one role serve all projects: the policy compares the principal's session tag against resource tags, granting project-scoped access dynamically. A shared role violates least privilege, resource tags alone don't constrain the principal, and SCPs are account-level guardrails rather than per-project grants.

q: A central logging bucket must accept writes from every account in the AWS Organization, including accounts created next month. Listing every account ID in the bucket policy means constant policy edits. Which condition key authorizes the whole organization at once?
options: aws:PrincipalAccount with a wildcard
aws:PrincipalOrgID — matches the organization ID, covering current and future member accounts
aws:SourceIp
s3:prefix
explain: aws:PrincipalOrgID matches the caller's organization, so one condition covers all present and future member accounts with no policy edits. PrincipalAccount takes specific account IDs (no wildcards), SourceIp is network-based rather than organization-based, and s3:prefix constrains object keys rather than callers.

q: A healthcare company must encrypt S3 objects with keys that AWS never stores or manages — the application supplies the key with each request and AWS must discard it afterward. Which encryption option meets this requirement?
options: SSE-C (server-side encryption with customer-provided keys) — the client sends the key per request and S3 never stores it
SSE-S3 with Amazon S3-managed keys
SSE-KMS with AWS-managed keys
Client-side encryption with keys in the application
explain: SSE-C performs server-side encryption using a key supplied in each request header, which S3 uses and then discards without storing. SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS both involve AWS-managed or AWS-stored keys, and client-side encryption encrypts before upload rather than server-side with a per-request key.

q: A bucket with heavy SSE-KMS write traffic generates millions of KMS API calls per month, and the KMS request charges are now significant. The team must keep KMS-based encryption with CloudTrail auditability. Which feature cuts the KMS request volume?
options: Disabling encryption on the bucket
Using one KMS key per object
S3 Bucket Keys — a per-bucket data key reduces calls to KMS for each object operation
Rotating the KMS key monthly
explain: S3 Bucket Keys cache a bucket-level data key so most operations don't call KMS, slashing request charges while keeping KMS-based encryption and CloudTrail key-usage logs. Disabling encryption abandons the requirement, per-object keys multiply KMS calls, and rotation changes key material rather than request volume.

q: An audit found unencrypted EBS volumes launched by developers who forgot to enable encryption. The security team wants encryption enforced automatically for every new volume and snapshot copy, with no reliance on developer diligence. Which setting provides this?
options: An IAM policy asking developers to encrypt
EBS encryption by default — enabled per account per Region, encrypting all new volumes and snapshot copies automatically
Encrypting volumes manually after launch
CloudTrail alerts on unencrypted volumes
explain: EBS encryption by default is an account/Region setting that encrypts every new EBS volume and snapshot copy with no per-launch action, closing the human-error gap. IAM policies can't directly force the encrypted flag without complex conditions, manual encryption is the diligence problem being fixed, and CloudTrail alerts are detective rather than preventive.

q: An engineer accidentally deletes a KMS key used by production databases. The team needs a safety window to detect the mistake and recover before the key material is destroyed. How does KMS handle key deletion?
options: Keys are deleted immediately and permanently
Keys can never be deleted
Key rotation replaces deletion
Scheduled deletion with a waiting period of 7 to 30 days — the deletion can be cancelled during the window
explain: KMS enforces a mandatory 7-to-30-day waiting period for scheduled key deletion, during which the deletion can be cancelled — the safety net for exactly this mistake. Immediate permanent deletion doesn't exist, keys can be deleted (with the waiting period), and rotation manages key material rather than preventing deletion.

q: A compliance policy requires cryptographic key rotation every year. The team uses KMS symmetric keys, asymmetric signing keys, and HMAC keys, and assumes automatic rotation covers all of them. Which statement is correct?
options: Automatic annual rotation applies to symmetric encryption KMS keys; asymmetric and HMAC keys must be rotated manually
Automatic rotation applies to every KMS key type
Rotation changes the key ID, breaking all references
KMS keys cannot be rotated
explain: KMS automatic rotation covers symmetric encryption keys (rotating the backing key material annually while the key ID and ARN stay the same); asymmetric and HMAC keys require manual rotation. The 'all key types' assumption is the exam trap, rotation never changes the key ID, and symmetric keys absolutely can rotate.

q: An incident response team needs to run SQL queries across two years of CloudTrail management and data events — filtering by user, IP, and error code — without building an Athena table or log pipeline first. Which service provides this?
options: CloudTrail event history, which only covers 90 days
S3 server access logging
CloudTrail Lake — a managed event data store with SQL querying over months or years of events
VPC Flow Logs
explain: CloudTrail Lake ingests events into a queryable store with built-in SQL, covering retention the team configures (up to years) with no pipeline to build. Event history caps at 90 days, S3 access logs record object access rather than API activity, and Flow Logs capture network metadata rather than CloudTrail events.

q: A company must continuously check its 40 accounts against the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark and remediate drift, with findings in one dashboard. Which service runs these automated compliance checks?
options: AWS Config rules alone, without aggregation
AWS Security Hub with the CIS and Foundational Security Best Practices standards enabled
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Artifact
explain: Security Hub runs automated checks against CIS and FSBP standards across accounts and aggregates pass/fail findings centrally. Config rules alone lack the aggregated compliance dashboard, GuardDuty detects threats rather than benchmark compliance, and Artifact hosts audit reports rather than running live checks.

q: A database team suspects brute-force login attempts against their Aurora clusters. GuardDuty is enabled, but no database findings appear. Which protection plan specifically monitors RDS/Aurora login activity for threats?
options: GuardDuty S3 Protection
GuardDuty EKS Protection
AWS WAF
GuardDuty RDS Protection — analyzes database login activity for anomalous and brute-force patterns
explain: RDS Protection is the GuardDuty plan that profiles login activity to Aurora and RDS instances to detect brute force and anomalous access. S3 Protection watches object API activity, EKS Protection watches Kubernetes audit logs, and WAF filters web requests — none monitor database logins.

q: A GuardDuty finding shows an EC2 instance communicating with a known malicious domain. Responders need to see which users, roles, and other resources interacted with that instance to scope the incident. Which service visualizes these entity relationships for investigation?
options: Amazon Detective — builds interactive graphs of users, instances, and API activity around a finding
AWS Security Hub
CloudTrail log file validation
Amazon Macie
explain: Detective ingests CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty findings into entity-relationship graphs so responders can pivot from the instance to the users and roles behind it. Security Hub aggregates findings without investigation graphs, log validation detects tampering, and Macie finds sensitive data in S3.

q: A legacy application role has a sprawling policy granting far more than it uses. The team wants to generate a tight replacement policy based on the role's actual API calls over the last 90 days, without hand-analyzing logs. Which feature builds this policy?
options: The IAM credential report
IAM Access Advisor alone, which only shows service usage
IAM Access Analyzer policy generation — analyzes CloudTrail activity and generates a least-privilege policy
Trusted Advisor
explain: Access Analyzer's policy generation consumes CloudTrail history and emits a scoped-down policy matching observed actions, automating least-privilege refactoring. The credential report shows credential age rather than action usage, Access Advisor shows last-accessed services without generating policies, and Trusted Advisor doesn't produce IAM policies.

q: A team creates a WAF web ACL in us-east-1 with regional scope and tries to attach it to their CloudFront distribution, but the distribution isn't listed as an available resource. What is wrong?
options: WAF cannot protect CloudFront at all
CloudFront requires a web ACL with CloudFront (global) scope, created in us-east-1 — regional-scope ACLs only attach to regional resources like ALB
The distribution needs an ALB in front of it
WAF rules take 24 hours to propagate
explain: WAF has two scopes: regional for ALB/API Gateway/AppSync and CloudFront (global) for distributions, and the ACL must be created in us-east-1 for CloudFront. A regional ACL simply can't attach to a distribution. WAF absolutely protects CloudFront, no ALB is needed in front, and propagation takes minutes rather than a day.

q: A three-tier application has web, app, and database tiers. The database security group currently allows MySQL from the entire app subnet CIDR, which also contains jump hosts that should never reach the database. Which approach restricts database access to only the app tier instances?
options: Opening the database security group to 0.0.0.0/0 with a strong password
A NACL blocking the jump hosts
Moving the jump hosts to the web tier
Security group referencing — allow port 3306 from the app tier's security group ID as the source
explain: Referencing the app tier's security group as the traffic source restricts access to exactly those instances, regardless of subnet layout, and stays correct as instances scale. Opening to the world is never acceptable, NACLs are subnet-level and can't single out instances, and moving jump hosts just relocates the problem.

q: A SaaS company exposes its service through AWS PrivateLink to enterprise customers, but wants to manually approve each customer's connection before traffic flows. Which PrivateLink configuration provides this control?
options: An endpoint service (backed by an NLB) with acceptance required — each connection request must be manually accepted
A public ALB with IP allowlisting
VPC peering with each customer
An interface endpoint with an open security group
explain: Endpoint services support 'acceptance required,' so the provider reviews and approves each consumer's connection request before connectivity is established. A public ALB exposes the service to the internet, VPC peering doesn't scale across customers and lacks approval workflow, and an open security group provides no approval gate.

q: A team issued an ACM certificate using DNS validation, then deleted the validation CNAME record during a DNS cleanup. Months later the certificate fails to auto-renew and the site faces an outage. What caused this?
options: ACM certificates never auto-renew
The private key expired
ACM must re-validate domain ownership at renewal — the CNAME record has to remain in place for automatic renewal
The certificate was used on too many resources
explain: ACM re-checks the DNS validation record before each automatic renewal, so deleting the CNAME breaks renewal even though the issued certificate was fine. ACM certificates do auto-renew when validation persists, private keys don't expire independently of the certificate, and usage count doesn't affect renewal.

q: An application in Account A needs to read a database password stored in Secrets Manager in Account B. The identity policy in Account A allows it, but access is still denied. What else is required?
options: Making the secret public
A resource-based policy on the secret in Account B granting the Account A principal access
VPC peering between the accounts
Copying the secret to Account A
explain: Secrets Manager supports resource-based policies, and cross-account access requires the secret's policy to grant the external principal — the identity policy alone isn't sufficient. Public secrets are never acceptable, VPC peering is irrelevant to Secrets Manager authorization, and copying secrets multiplies rotation burden.

q: A mobile app lets guests browse the catalog without signing in, but guests should only read public product data while signed-in users get broader access. Which Cognito identity pool configuration supports both tiers?
options: A user pool with MFA required for everyone
IAM users for each guest
One role for all users
Enable unauthenticated identities with a restricted guest role, plus an authenticated role with broader permissions for signed-in users
explain: Identity pools distinguish authenticated from unauthenticated identities, assigning each a different IAM role — least privilege for guests, broader access for members. Requiring MFA for guests defeats guest access, IAM users per guest is unmanageable, and one role for everyone gives guests the same power as members.

q: A company with an on-premises Active Directory wants EC2 and AWS applications to authenticate against it, without deploying a full managed AD in AWS. Which directory service option proxies authentication to the existing on-premises AD?
options: AD Connector — forwards directory requests to the on-premises Active Directory
AWS Managed Microsoft AD
Simple AD
IAM Identity Center alone
explain: AD Connector is a directory gateway that proxies authentication to the existing on-premises AD with no data replication into AWS. Managed Microsoft AD deploys a full separate AD forest, Simple AD is a standalone Samba-based directory, and Identity Center provides SSO rather than AD proxying.

q: A security team writes an SCP denying ec2:RunInstances without encrypted volumes, expecting it to apply to every account including the management account. Which accounts and principals does the SCP actually affect?
options: Every account and every principal including root
Only the management account
All member accounts except the management account, and it never applies to service-linked roles
Only IAM users, not roles
explain: SCPs apply to member accounts but never to the management account, and they don't affect service-linked roles — both are documented exclusions teams forget. The 'applies to everything including root in all accounts' assumption is the classic trap; SCPs also apply equally to users and roles in member accounts.

q: A platform team wants all product accounts to launch workloads into centrally managed shared subnets, so network addressing stays consistent and security controls apply uniformly. Creating identical VPCs in each account causes drift. Which service shares the subnets across accounts?
options: VPC peering between every account
AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) — share subnets (and other resources) from the network account with member accounts
Transit Gateway
Copying the VPC with CloudFormation
explain: RAM shares actual subnets from the central network account into member accounts (VPC sharing), so addressing and controls stay uniform with no duplication. Peering connects separate VPCs rather than sharing subnets, Transit Gateway routes between VPCs rather than sharing them, and copied VPCs drift apart over time.

q: On-premises servers need temporary AWS credentials to upload logs to S3. The security team forbids long-term access keys on these servers. The servers already have X.509 certificates from the corporate CA. Which service exchanges those certificates for temporary AWS credentials?
options: IAM users with access keys rotated monthly
AD Connector
AWS Client VPN
IAM Roles Anywhere — uses X.509 certificates with a trust anchor to vend temporary credentials to non-AWS workloads
explain: IAM Roles Anywhere lets on-premises workloads present X.509 certificates to assume IAM roles and receive temporary credentials — no long-term keys stored on the servers. Monthly-rotated keys are still long-term credentials, AD Connector handles directory authentication rather than AWS credentials, and Client VPN provides network access rather than credentials.

q: A penetration test shows the EC2 metadata service can be reached through an SSRF vulnerability in the application. The team wants metadata requests to require a session token. They also run containers, which need a hop limit of 2. Which configuration addresses this?
options: Enforce IMDSv2 (token-required metadata) and set the hop limit to 2 for containerized workloads
Disable the metadata service entirely
Block 169.254.169.254 in the security group
Use IMDSv1 with a hop limit of 1
explain: IMDSv2 requires a PUT-generated session token, defeating simple SSRF GET requests against the metadata service, and containers need the hop limit raised to 2 because packets traverse an extra hop. Disabling metadata breaks IAM role credential delivery, security groups can't filter link-local metadata traffic, and IMDSv1 is the vulnerable mode being replaced.

q: A support engineer needs to download one private S3 object to diagnose a customer issue. Creating an IAM user for this one-off access is overkill, and the bucket must stay private. Which approach grants temporary, scoped access to just that object?
options: Making the object public temporarily
A bucket policy allowing the engineer's home IP
A presigned URL with a short expiration — temporary authenticated access to the specific object
Emailing the object as an attachment
explain: A presigned URL grants time-limited access to exactly one object using the signer's permissions, with no bucket changes or new identities. Temporary public access risks exposure and caching, IP-based bucket policies are coarse and linger, and emailing customer data creates an uncontrolled copy.

q: A company serves premium video through CloudFront from a private S3 bucket. Subscribers should access content via CloudFront, but direct S3 URLs must never work and non-subscribers must be blocked at the edge. Which combination enforces this?
options: OAC on the S3 origin alone
CloudFront signed URLs or signed cookies for viewer authorization, plus Origin Access Control so S3 only accepts CloudFront requests
WAF rate-based rules alone
Public bucket with CloudFront in front
explain: Signed URLs/cookies authenticate viewers at the edge (blocking non-subscribers), while OAC ensures the bucket only serves CloudFront — never direct S3 URLs. OAC alone protects the origin but doesn't authorize viewers, WAF rate rules don't do subscriber authentication, and a public bucket defeats the entire model.

q: A company buys Compute Savings Plans expecting guaranteed EC2 capacity during an AZ capacity shortage, but their launches still fail with insufficient-capacity errors. What should they understand about Savings Plans?
options: Savings Plans are a billing discount only — they reserve no capacity; guaranteed launches need zonal Reserved Instances or On-Demand Capacity Reservations
Savings Plans guarantee capacity in all AZs
Switching to Convertible RIs adds capacity guarantees
Spot Instances provide the missing guarantee
explain: Savings Plans discount the bill for matching usage but reserve nothing — capacity guarantees come only from zonal RIs or On-Demand Capacity Reservations. Expecting launch guarantees from a billing construct is the misconception; Convertible RIs are still billing constructs, and Spot offers the least capacity assurance of all.

q: Before launching a large Spot fleet for a weekend rendering job, the team wants to know which instance types and AZs are most likely to actually fulfill the Spot request. Which tool answers this in advance?
options: Spot price history alone
CloudWatch CPU metrics
EC2 Spot placement score — estimates the likelihood of request fulfillment per instance type and AZ
Launching a test fleet and watching
explain: The Spot placement score API scores instance type and AZ combinations on expected fulfillment success, letting the team choose pools likely to deliver. Price history shows cost rather than availability, CPU metrics describe running instances rather than spare capacity, and test launches waste time and money.

q: An Auto Scaling group lists 14 approved instance types, and every new generation forces a template update. The team wants to declare requirements (4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM, Nitro) and let EC2 pick matching types automatically. Which feature supports this?
options: A launch template per instance type
Attribute-based instance type selection — specify vCPU, memory, and other attributes instead of enumerating types
Manual instance launches
A single fixed instance type
explain: Attribute-based instance type selection expresses requirements as attributes, so new generations matching the attributes are picked up automatically with no template churn. Per-type templates multiply maintenance, manual launches abandon automation, and a single fixed type concentrates Spot interruption risk.

q: A versioned S3 bucket's lifecycle rule deletes noncurrent versions after 90 days, but storage keeps growing. Investigation shows millions of delete markers with no live objects behind them. Which lifecycle action cleans these up?
options: Deleting all object versions immediately
Disabling versioning on the bucket
Transitioning delete markers to Glacier
A lifecycle rule to delete expired object delete markers — removes markers whose noncurrent versions have all expired
explain: The 'delete expired object delete markers' lifecycle action removes markers left behind after their versions expired, which plain noncurrent-version expiration leaves orphaned. Deleting all versions destroys data the policy intended to keep 90 days, disabling versioning doesn't remove existing markers, and delete markers can't transition to Glacier.

q: A data governance team needs a full inventory of 80 million S3 objects — sizes, storage classes, encryption status — to find lifecycle gaps and unencrypted objects. ListObjects calls would take days and throttle. Which feature produces this report?
options: S3 Inventory — scheduled CSV/Parquet reports of bucket objects and metadata
S3 Storage Lens
CloudTrail data events
Manual console browsing
explain: S3 Inventory generates scheduled object-level reports with metadata like storage class and encryption status, designed for exactly this audit at scale. Storage Lens gives aggregated metrics rather than per-object lists, CloudTrail records API activity rather than object inventories, and console browsing can't handle 80 million objects.

q: A database team provisioned io1 volumes with 10,000 IOPS two years ago, but monitoring shows actual usage never exceeds 2,000 IOPS. They're paying premium provisioned-IOPS rates for headroom they don't need. Which change cuts cost without downtime?
options: Adding more io1 volumes
Switching to io2 Block Express
Modify the volumes to gp3 with 2,000-3,000 provisioned IOPS — gp3 delivers the needed IOPS at a fraction of io1 cost, live via elastic volumes
Taking more snapshots
explain: gp3 decouples IOPS from the volume and prices them far below io1, so 2,000-3,000 provisioned IOPS on gp3 covers actual usage cheaply with a live modification. More io1 volumes deepen the overpayment, io2 Block Express is even pricier per IOPS, and snapshots don't change volume pricing.

q: A company is adopting IPv6 and wants instances in private subnets to reach the internet for updates, without paying NAT gateway data processing charges. Which gateway provides outbound-only internet access for IPv6?
options: An internet gateway on the private subnets
An egress-only internet gateway — outbound IPv6 traffic without inbound connections and without NAT charges
A NAT gateway, which handles IPv6
A transit gateway
explain: An egress-only internet gateway lets IPv6 instances initiate outbound connections while blocking inbound ones, with no per-GB processing charge like NAT gateways. An internet gateway on private subnets would allow inbound traffic, NAT gateways are IPv4-only constructs with processing fees, and Transit Gateway routes between networks rather than to the internet.

q: Two chatty VPCs exchange 30 TB/month through a Transit Gateway, and the bill shows large Transit Gateway data processing charges. The VPCs are in the same Region and same organization. Which connectivity change removes the per-GB processing charge?
options: Adding a second Transit Gateway
Routing through a NAT gateway
Using Direct Connect between the VPCs
VPC peering — no per-GB processing charge, unlike Transit Gateway
explain: VPC peering carries no hourly or per-GB processing charge (standard data transfer rates still apply), while Transit Gateway bills per-GB processing on top. More Transit Gateways multiply the charges, NAT gateways add their own processing fees, and Direct Connect connects on-premises networks rather than VPC to VPC.

q: A DynamoDB table has four global secondary indexes created during past experiments. Only one is queried now, but the table's write costs are triple what the base table alone would cost. What is the likely waste?
options: Delete the three unused GSIs — each GSI consumes its own write capacity and storage even when never queried
Enable DynamoDB Streams
Switch the table to on-demand mode
Add DAX
explain: Every GSI replicates writes and stores its own projected copy, so three idle GSIs silently multiply write and storage costs. Streams add change capture rather than removing index cost, on-demand mode doesn't eliminate GSI charges, and DAX caches reads without touching index costs.

q: A Lambda function was configured with 10 GB of ephemeral storage for a data-processing task, and the bill shows a new Lambda storage charge the team didn't expect. How is Lambda ephemeral storage billed?
options: All ephemeral storage is free
Only memory affects the bill
Storage beyond the included 512 MB is billed — the extra ~9.5 GB incurs charges
Ephemeral storage is billed per invocation
explain: Lambda includes 512 MB of ephemeral storage free; anything configured above that is billed for the provisioned amount. The team assumed storage was free like the default, but the 10 GB configuration added a real line item. Memory is billed separately per millisecond, and the charge is for provisioned capacity rather than per invocation.

q: A team enabled RDS Performance Insights with 2-year data retention for trend analysis, then noticed a new Performance Insights charge on the bill. They assumed it was entirely free. What is the actual pricing?
options: Performance Insights is free at any retention
7 days of performance data retention is free; longer retention is billed
It is only free for Aurora
Disabling Multi-AZ removes the charge
explain: Performance Insights includes 7 days of retention free, with paid tiers for extended history — the 2-year setting is what generated the charge. It isn't free-unlimited, the free tier covers RDS and Aurora alike, and Multi-AZ is unrelated to Performance Insights pricing.

q: An Aurora cluster's bill shows I/O charges making up 40% of the total database cost, and I/O keeps growing with the workload. Standard Aurora bills per million I/Os. Which configuration is likely cheaper here?
options: A larger DB instance class
More Aurora Replicas
Aurora Serverless v1
Aurora I/O-Optimized — predictable pricing that wins when I/O charges exceed roughly 25% of the total bill
explain: AWS documents I/O-Optimized as the cheaper choice once I/O charges pass about 25% of total DB cost — at 40% this workload is well past that line. Bigger instances don't change the per-I/O billing, replicas add read capacity rather than cheaper I/O, and Serverless v1 has its own pricing that doesn't target I/O-heavy provisioned workloads.

q: An analytics team queries Redshift for a few hours each week, but the provisioned cluster bills 24/7. Pausing and resuming manually is forgotten half the time. Which option bills only for queries actually run?
options: Redshift Serverless — pay per query with automatic scaling and no cluster to manage
A larger RA3 cluster
Concurrency scaling always on
A single-node DC2 cluster
explain: Redshift Serverless charges for the compute used during queries and scales automatically, eliminating both the 24/7 cluster bill and the manual pause discipline. A bigger cluster deepens the idle waste, always-on concurrency scaling adds burst charges, and a single-node cluster still bills around the clock.

q: A company runs nightly Glue ETL jobs that are not time-sensitive — they just need to finish before morning. Standard Glue DPUs feel overpriced for flexible work. Which execution class lowers the cost of non-urgent jobs?
options: Glue Standard, the default
More DPUs for faster completion
Glue Flex — a lower-cost execution class for non-urgent, flexible ETL workloads
Glue DataBrew
explain: Glue Flex trades scheduling flexibility for a lower DPU-hour price, fitting overnight jobs with soft deadlines. Standard is the full-price default, more DPUs speed the job without lowering the unit price, and DataBrew is an interactive data-prep tool rather than a cheaper execution class.

q: A Firehose delivery stream writes millions of tiny files to S3 each day, and the downstream Athena queries are slow and expensive because of S3 request overhead on small files. Which Firehose feature reduces the file count by organizing records inline?
options: Increasing the buffer interval alone
Dynamic partitioning — partition records by keys like date inline, producing fewer, better-organized S3 objects
Adding a Lambda transformation
Switching to Kinesis Data Streams
explain: Dynamic partitioning groups records by partition keys before delivery, cutting the tiny-file sprawl and the S3 request costs that come with it, while also speeding Athena queries. Buffer tuning alone can't organize by key, a Lambda transform adds cost without partitioning, and Data Streams reintroduces shard management.

q: A startup's Kafka traffic is bursty — quiet for days, then event-driven spikes. A provisioned MSK cluster idles between spikes, and self-managing Kafka is out of the question. Which MSK option bills only for actual throughput and storage?
options: A larger provisioned MSK cluster
MSK with more broker nodes
Self-managed Kafka on Spot Instances
MSK Serverless — no brokers to size, pay per throughput and storage used
explain: MSK Serverless removes broker sizing entirely and bills on actual throughput and storage, matching the bursty pattern with no idle capacity. Bigger or more-broker clusters deepen the idle waste, and self-managed Kafka on Spot trades the managed service away while adding operational burden.

q: A team believes Savings Plans only cover EC2 and is buying separate commitments for Fargate and Lambda. What should they know about Compute Savings Plans coverage?
options: Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2, Fargate, and Lambda usage — one commitment covers all three
Savings Plans are EC2-only
Fargate and Lambda need Reserved Instances
Each service needs its own Savings Plan type
explain: Compute Savings Plans flex across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda, so a single commitment discounts all three — no separate purchases needed. EC2 Instance Savings Plans are the EC2-family-specific variant, Reserved Instances don't exist for Fargate or Lambda, and splitting commitments fragments the discount.

q: A CloudFront distribution serves 2 TB/month of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Data transfer dominates the distribution's cost. Which built-in feature shrinks these text responses and the transfer bill?
options: Longer TTLs
Signed URLs
Automatic object compression — CloudFront compresses compressible content at the edge, reducing bytes transferred
More origin servers
explain: CloudFront's automatic compression gzips text-based responses at the edge, directly cutting transferred bytes and the transfer bill. Longer TTLs reduce origin fetches but not the bytes served to viewers, signed URLs control access rather than size, and more origins add cost without shrinking responses.

q: A team enabled S3 Transfer Acceleration on every bucket 'for faster uploads,' including buckets whose uploaders sit in the same Region. The bill now shows Transfer Acceleration charges with no speed benefit. When is the feature actually worth its surcharge?
options: It is free, so the charges are a billing error
Transfer Acceleration adds a per-GB surcharge and only helps long-distance uploads over the public internet — same-Region uploads gain nothing
It replaces CloudFront
It reduces S3 storage costs
explain: Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through CloudFront edge locations for a per-GB surcharge, which pays off only for distant uploaders on slow internet paths; same-Region uploads see no benefit for the extra fee. It isn't free, it doesn't replace CloudFront distributions, and it affects transfer rather than storage pricing.

q: A company manages EC2 and RDS backups centrally with AWS Backup plans. Compliance requires 7-year retention of all recovery points, but anything older than 6 months is almost never restored. Standard backup storage for 7 years is expensive. Which AWS Backup feature lowers the cost of the aging recovery points?
options: Deleting recovery points after 6 months
Copying recovery points to more Regions
More frequent backups
Backup cold storage tier — transition aging recovery points to lower-cost storage with slower restore
explain: AWS Backup's cold storage tier moves older recovery points to cheaper storage while keeping them restorable, matching the rarely-restored retention requirement. Deleting violates the 7-year rule, more regional copies multiply cost, and frequent backups increase rather than reduce storage spend.

q: A build farm on EFS has wildly bursty throughput — idle most of the hour, then huge spikes. Provisioned throughput sized for the spikes is expensive, and bursting credits run dry. Which EFS throughput mode fits unpredictable bursts without provisioning?
options: Elastic throughput — automatically scales throughput up and down with actual activity, pay per use
Maximum provisioned throughput
Bursting mode with larger file systems
EFS One Zone
explain: Elastic throughput scales with real-time demand and bills on usage, handling unpredictable spikes without provisioned capacity or credit math. Maximum provisioned throughput is the expensive pattern they're escaping, bursting credits are exactly what runs dry, and One Zone changes durability scope rather than throughput mode.

q: A machine learning team runs training jobs on FSx for Lustre. The training data is re-downloaded from S3 for every run, so the file system is purely temporary scratch. Which deployment type is cheapest for this throwaway data?
options: Persistent file system with replication
FSx for Windows File Server
Scratch file system — no data replication, lower cost for temporary processing data
EFS Standard
explain: Scratch file systems skip data replication for lower cost, which is ideal when the data is re-fetched from S3 each run and loss is inconsequential. Persistent deployment pays for replication the workload doesn't need, FSx for Windows is the wrong protocol, and EFS Standard is a different performance and price profile for shared POSIX storage.

q: A company transfers 100 TB/month between its data center and AWS over a Site-to-Site VPN. At this volume, per-GB internet data transfer pricing is becoming painful. Which connectivity change typically lowers the per-GB transfer cost at scale?
options: A bigger VPN tunnel
AWS Direct Connect — lower per-GB data transfer rates than internet-based transfer at high volumes, plus consistent performance
More NAT gateways
CloudFront for the transfers
explain: Direct Connect offers reduced per-GB data transfer pricing compared to internet egress, which compounds into real savings at 100 TB/month, alongside consistent throughput. A bigger VPN tunnel still rides internet-priced transfer, NAT gateways add processing charges, and CloudFront serves content outward rather than hybrid transfer.

q: A development environment's Auto Scaling group runs 10 instances 24/7 but is only used during business hours. Terminating nightly loses warm caches the team wants to keep. Which approach stops the spend nights and weekends while preserving the instances?
options: Deleting the Auto Scaling group nightly
Moving to Spot Instances only
Manual termination by developers
Scheduled scaling actions — scale desired capacity to zero on a schedule and back up in the morning
explain: Scheduled scaling sets desired capacity to zero nights and weekends and restores it before business hours — no instances running means no compute charges, and the morning scale-out rebuilds the fleet. Deleting the group destroys configuration, Spot alone still bills for running hours, and manual termination is unreliable toil.

q: A cleanup finds 200 deregistered AMIs from old CI builds, but the EBS snapshots behind them are still in the account and still billing. The team assumed deleting the AMI removed everything. What is the correct cleanup?
options: Deregister the AMI and delete its associated EBS snapshots — deregistration alone leaves snapshots (and their charges) behind
Do nothing; snapshots expire automatically
Delete the snapshots only, keeping the AMIs
Convert the snapshots to AMIs again
explain: Deregistering an AMI does not delete its backing EBS snapshots, which keep billing until explicitly deleted — both steps are required for full cleanup. Snapshots never expire on their own, deleting snapshots while keeping AMIs breaks the images, and re-converting snapshots just recreates the clutter.

q: After a ransomware incident at a peer company, a CTO wants backups that remain recoverable even if attackers gain administrative access to the AWS account and try to delete them. Which AWS Backup feature provides immutable, undeletable recovery points?
options: Standard backup vaults with default settings
Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode, which blocks deletion of recovery points until the retention period expires
Cross-account backup copies to a second account
Enabling MFA on the root user account
explain: Vault Lock in compliance mode makes recovery points immutable — not even the root user can delete them before retention expires, which defeats ransomware deletion attempts. Standard vaults and cross-account copies can still be deleted by a compromised admin, and root MFA protects the root login, not backup deletion by other admins.

q: A compliance policy requires every EC2 instance to be replaced with a freshly patched AMI at least every 90 days, but the Auto Scaling group only replaces instances during scaling events. Which setting enforces automatic periodic instance refresh regardless of scaling activity?
options: Scheduled scaling actions every 90 days
Suspending the health check replacement process
Maximum instance lifetime, which terminates and replaces instances after the configured age (7 days to 1 year)
Instance refresh with a 0% minimum healthy percentage
explain: Maximum instance lifetime automatically recycles instances once they reach the configured age (between 7 days and 1 year), enforcing patch freshness without manual intervention. Scheduled scaling only changes capacity, suspending health checks weakens resilience, and instance refresh with 0% minimum healthy would take the whole fleet down at once.

q: A disaster recovery runbook restores 4 TB EBS volumes from snapshots, but the first access to restored data is painfully slow because blocks are lazily loaded from S3. The RTO requires restored volumes to be fully performant immediately. Which feature should the team enable on critical snapshots?
options: EBS Fast Snapshot Restore, which pre-warms snapshots in selected AZs so restored volumes deliver full performance at creation
EBS encryption by default
Snapshot archiving to the archive tier
Increasing the snapshot copy throughput limit
explain: Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) pre-initializes snapshot blocks in chosen Availability Zones, so volumes created from those snapshots are fully performant immediately instead of warming lazily from S3. Encryption by default doesn't change restore performance, the archive tier makes restores slower and costlier, and there is no snapshot copy throughput limit to raise.

q: A company runs its application active-passive across two Regions behind ALBs. They need DNS to automatically stop sending traffic to the primary Region when its ALB health checks fail, with no manual intervention. Which Route 53 configuration achieves this?
options: Weighted routing with equal weights
Geolocation routing with a default record
Latency-based routing between the two ALBs
Failover routing with health checks on alias records pointing to each ALB
explain: Failover routing with Route 53 health checks on alias records automatically shifts DNS answers to the secondary ALB when the primary fails its checks. Weighted routing splits traffic rather than failing over, geolocation routes by user location, and latency-based routing picks the lowest-latency endpoint without health-driven failover.

q: A team runs an Aurora Global Database and needs to perform planned maintenance on the primary Region with minimal downtime. They want AWS to orchestrate the promotion of a secondary Region rather than running manual steps. Which approach gives the fastest, AWS-managed regional failover?
options: Deleting the primary cluster and recreating it in the secondary Region
Managed failover of the Aurora Global Database, which promotes a secondary Region typically in under a minute
Restoring the latest snapshot into the secondary Region
Enabling S3 cross-region replication for the database files
explain: Managed failover for Aurora Global Database promotes a secondary cluster to primary in typically under a minute with no data loss beyond in-flight replication. Deleting and recreating the primary is destructive, snapshot restore takes far longer and loses recent writes, and databases don't replicate via S3 replication.

q: A team must upgrade its production RDS for PostgreSQL engine version with near-zero downtime and a fast rollback option if the new version misbehaves. Which RDS feature creates a synchronized staging environment and switches over in typically under a minute?
options: A read replica promoted manually during a maintenance window
Restoring from a snapshot into a new instance
RDS Blue/Green deployments, which keep a fully synced green environment and switchover typically completes in under a minute
Multi-AZ failover triggered on demand
explain: Blue/Green deployments maintain a synchronized green copy of production; switchover typically completes in under a minute and the blue environment remains available for instant rollback. Manual replica promotion is slower and error-prone, snapshot restore loses recent data and takes longer, and Multi-AZ failover doesn't change engine versions.

q: An application writes to an Aurora Global Database from both the primary and a secondary Region. The team wants secondary-Region writes to succeed without the application redirecting connections across Regions. Which feature enables this?
options: Aurora write forwarding, which lets a secondary cluster forward write operations to the primary cluster
Aurora Backtrack on the secondary cluster
Enabling Multi-AZ on the secondary cluster
Creating a read replica in the secondary Region
explain: Write forwarding allows applications connected to a secondary Region's Aurora cluster to issue writes that are forwarded to the primary, removing the need for cross-region connection logic. Backtrack rewinds data rather than forwarding writes, Multi-AZ is intra-region failover, and read replicas accept no writes.

q: During an incident, one Availability Zone shows degraded EC2 performance but hasn't fully failed, so automated health checks keep sending it traffic. The team wants to immediately shift application traffic away from that AZ for up to 3 days while they investigate. Which Application Recovery Controller feature does this?
options: Routing control state changes
Readiness checks
Creating a new Route 53 hosted zone
Zonal shift, which moves traffic away from an impaired AZ for a configurable duration up to 3 days
explain: Zonal shift evacuates traffic from a specific AZ for up to 3 days without requiring full failover, ideal for gray-failure scenarios where health checks still pass. Routing controls shift traffic between Regions or cells, readiness checks only assess preparedness, and a new hosted zone doesn't move traffic.

q: A company pages on-call engineers whenever any single EC2 CPU alarm fires, causing alert fatigue from transient spikes. They want a single alarm that fires only when multiple underlying conditions are simultaneously true. Which CloudWatch feature supports this?
options: CloudWatch Logs Insights queries
Composite alarms, which combine multiple alarms with boolean logic so notification fires only when the combined state warrants it
Increasing the alarm evaluation period to one hour
Disabling all CPU alarms below 95%
explain: Composite alarms aggregate multiple alarms using AND/OR logic, so paging triggers only when several signals agree — sharply reducing noise from transient single-metric spikes. Logs Insights analyzes log data rather than alarming, longer evaluation periods delay real incidents too, and disabling alarms blinds the team to genuine problems.

q: A company is migrating Windows file shares that require the SMB protocol and Active Directory integration, and the shares must survive an AZ failure automatically. Which storage service provides managed, Multi-AZ SMB file shares?
options: Amazon EFS with mount targets in each AZ
Amazon S3 with SMB gateway endpoints
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with Multi-AZ deployment, which automatically fails over file shares to the standby AZ
Amazon EBS volumes shared via NFS
explain: FSx for Windows File Server is purpose-built for SMB with AD integration, and Multi-AZ deployment provides automatic failover of the file system to the standby AZ. EFS is NFS-only with no native SMB, S3 is object storage without an SMB protocol, and EBS volumes can't be shared between instances for file serving.

q: A company uses Amazon EFS for shared content in us-east-1 and needs continuous cross-region replication so a regional outage doesn't halt content delivery, with recovery measured in minutes. Which EFS capability meets this?
options: EFS replication, which continuously replicates file system data to a second Region with minutes-level RPO and RTO
EFS lifecycle management to Infrequent Access
Copying files with AWS DataSync on a nightly schedule
EFS access points for application isolation
explain: EFS replication continuously copies data to a destination file system in another Region with minutes-level RPO/RTO, designed exactly for regional DR. Lifecycle management only changes storage class, nightly DataSync copies leave up to 24 hours of data loss, and access points control permissions rather than replicating data.

q: A session store runs on Amazon MemoryDB in a single AZ. The team needs automatic failover to a standby replica with minimal data loss if the primary fails. Which MemoryDB characteristic provides this?
options: MemoryDB snapshots copied manually to another AZ
Enabling cluster mode for sharding
Using Redis data tiering to S3
MemoryDB Multi-AZ with automatic failover to a replica, providing a durable in-memory database with fast failover
explain: MemoryDB is Multi-AZ by design with automatic failover to standby replicas, keeping the in-memory dataset durable and available without manual promotion. Manual snapshot copies are slow and lossy, cluster mode scales throughput rather than adding failover, and data tiering optimizes cost rather than availability.

q: An operator accidentally deleted critical items from a DynamoDB table 10 days ago. The team needs to restore the table to its state just before the deletion without having configured any backups. Which feature makes this possible?
options: DynamoDB on-demand backup snapshots
Point-in-time recovery, which retains continuous backups for 35 days and can restore to any second within that window
DynamoDB Streams replay
Exporting the table to S3 and reimporting
explain: Point-in-time recovery keeps 35 days of continuous backups and restores the table to any second in that window — no prior snapshot configuration needed beyond enabling PITR. On-demand backups only capture the moment they're taken, Streams retain just 24 hours, and export/import reflects current (already damaged) data.

q: A financial services firm replicates critical objects cross-region with S3 replication and has a compliance requirement that 99.9% of objects replicate within 15 minutes. Which S3 feature provides a backed SLA for replication time?
options: S3 Versioning on both buckets
S3 Inventory reports
S3 Replication Time Control (RTC), which replicates most objects in seconds backed by a 15-minute SLA
Enabling Transfer Acceleration on the destination bucket
explain: Replication Time Control provides an SLA that 99.9% of objects replicate within 15 minutes (typically seconds), which is what compliance needs. Versioning is a prerequisite but gives no timing guarantee, Inventory only reports object lists, and Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads rather than replication.

q: A legacy application keeps critical state in RAM and on the instance store, so it cannot survive a stop/start cycle. The team wants to stop instances overnight to save cost while preserving the full in-memory state. Which EC2 feature supports this?
options: EC2 hibernation, which saves RAM contents to the EBS root volume so the instance resumes exactly where it stopped
EC2 Auto Scaling scheduled actions
EBS snapshots of the root volume
Instance store-backed AMIs
explain: Hibernation persists RAM to the EBS root volume on stop and restores it on start, so the OS and applications resume in place — unlike a normal stop which wipes RAM. Scheduled actions only change capacity, snapshots capture disk but not running memory state, and instance store data is lost on stop regardless of AMI type.

q: An ALB spans three AZs, but nearly all registered targets are in one AZ, and a client-side DNS cache pins users to a single ALB node IP, overloading that AZ. Which ALB setting fixes the uneven distribution?
options: Enabling sticky sessions on the target group
Switching the ALB to a Network Load Balancer
Reducing the ALB idle timeout
Enabling cross-zone load balancing so each ALB node distributes evenly across targets in all AZs
explain: Cross-zone load balancing lets every load balancer node route to targets in all enabled AZs, smoothing out the imbalance caused by DNS caching pinning clients to one node. Sticky sessions worsen imbalance, switching LB types doesn't address distribution, and idle timeout controls connection lifetime rather than routing.

q: A hybrid architecture needs on-premises servers to resolve private Route 53 records for VPC resources, and VPC resources need to resolve on-premises DNS names. Which Route 53 Resolver components provide this bidirectional hybrid DNS?
options: Route 53 public hosted zones with NS delegation
Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints, forwarding queries in both directions between on-premises DNS and Route 53
Route 53 health checks on the on-premises DNS servers
Enabling DNS hostnames on the VPC only
explain: Resolver inbound endpoints let on-premises DNS forward queries for AWS private names into the VPC, while outbound endpoints let VPC resources forward on-premises names outward — together they provide bidirectional hybrid resolution. Public hosted zones expose records to the internet, health checks monitor rather than resolve, and DNS hostnames alone don't bridge on-premises DNS.

q: A team manages EC2 and RDS backups centrally and must prove every protected resource meets its backup policy, with automated remediation when a resource drifts out of compliance. Which combination provides centralized backup governance?
options: Manual snapshots with calendar reminders
AWS Backup Audit Manager with backup plans and AWS Config rules, providing compliance reporting and automated remediation
Copying snapshots to S3 buckets monthly
Enabling CloudTrail data events on backup APIs
explain: AWS Backup Audit Manager continuously evaluates backup plan compliance across resources with Config rules, reports, and automated remediation when resources drift. Manual snapshots don't scale or self-audit, S3 copies aren't managed backups, and CloudTrail only logs API calls rather than enforcing backup policy.

q: An EventBridge rule invokes a Lambda function for each order event. When the Lambda's downstream database had an outage, events processed during the outage were lost forever. How can the team replay those missed events after recovery?
options: EventBridge event archives with replay, which store published events and allow replaying them to the event bus for a retention period
Increasing the Lambda function's timeout
Enabling Lambda provisioned concurrency
Turning on CloudWatch detailed monitoring
explain: Event archives durably store events sent to the bus and support replaying a time range back through the rules, recovering exactly the events missed during the outage. Longer timeouts don't help a down database, provisioned concurrency addresses cold starts, and detailed monitoring only improves metric granularity.

q: A database team needs full production-like copies of a 3 TB Aurora cluster for load testing, but snapshot restores take hours and double storage costs during each test cycle. Which Aurora feature creates a fast, space-efficient copy?
options: Aurora Global Database secondary clusters
Aurora Serverless v2 scaling
Cross-region snapshot copy
Aurora cloning, which creates a copy-on-write clone in minutes that initially consumes no additional storage
explain: Aurora cloning uses copy-on-write so a full cluster copy is available in minutes with near-zero initial storage cost, ideal for disposable test environments. Global Database secondaries are for DR not testing, Serverless v2 scales compute rather than cloning data, and cross-region copies are slow and full-cost.

q: An application experiences sudden traffic surges, and new EC2 instances take 6 minutes to install software before serving traffic, causing errors during the surge. Which Auto Scaling feature keeps pre-initialized instances ready for instant scale-out?
options: Larger instance types for faster boot
Warm pools, which maintain stopped or running pre-initialized instances that can enter service in seconds during scale-out
Disabling all lifecycle hooks
Setting the health check grace period to zero
explain: Warm pools keep instances with software already installed in a stopped or hibernated state, so scale-out brings them into service in seconds instead of waiting through a 6-minute install. Larger instances still run the same install, disabling lifecycle hooks removes graceful handling, and a zero grace period causes premature health-check failures.

q: A company uses Route 53 weighted routing to split traffic 70/30 between two Regions, but wants the 70% Region to automatically drain if its application health degrades, even though its ALB still responds to TCP checks. Which health check design detects application-level failure?
options: Route 53 health checks against the ALB's IP addresses only
Geoproximity routing with bias
Health checks against an application endpoint that returns failure when the app is unhealthy, combined with CloudWatch alarm-based calculated health checks
Increasing the DNS TTL to 3600 seconds
explain: Application-endpoint health checks (plus CloudWatch metric-based calculated checks) detect real application degradation that TCP checks miss, letting Route 53 drain the failing Region automatically. IP-only checks pass while the app is broken, geoproximity adjusts geography rather than health, and a long TTL slows failover instead of enabling it.

q: A company's primary site runs on EC2 behind an ALB in us-east-1. For regional failover they want CloudFront to automatically serve traffic from a standby ALB in us-west-2 when the primary origin fails health checks. Which CloudFront configuration provides automatic origin failover?
options: A CloudFront origin group with the primary ALB and the standby ALB, failing over when the primary returns configured error status codes
Two separate CloudFront distributions, one per Region
Increasing the CloudFront default TTL
Signed URLs on the primary origin
explain: Origin groups define primary and secondary origins with failover criteria, so CloudFront automatically retries the standby ALB when the primary fails — no DNS changes needed. Two distributions require manual cutover, TTL controls caching rather than failover, and signed URLs control access rather than availability.

q: A company runs RDS for PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ, but application failover still takes minutes because the app must discover the new primary and re-establish hundreds of connections. Which proxy service transparently preserves connections during failover?
options: An NLB in front of the RDS endpoint
A Route 53 failover record
ElastiCache for Redis as a session store
Amazon RDS Proxy, which pools connections and can reduce failover times by up to 66% by routing to the new primary without app reconnection storms
explain: RDS Proxy maintains the connection pool and transparently routes to the promoted primary during failover, cutting failover time by up to 66% and sparing the app a reconnection storm. An NLB can't track database topology, Route 53 DNS failover is slowed by TTL caching, and Redis sessions don't fix connection re-establishment.

q: Before a major product launch, a team wants to validate that its multi-AZ architecture actually survives AZ impairment by deliberately injecting faults in a controlled, reversible way. Which AWS service runs controlled chaos experiments?
options: AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS), which injects faults like AZ network disruption or instance termination in controlled experiments with guardrails
AWS Config conformance packs
Amazon Inspector network assessments
CloudWatch Synthetics canaries
explain: AWS Fault Injection Service is the purpose-built chaos engineering service for controlled fault experiments with safety guardrails and automatic rollback. Config checks configuration compliance, Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, and Synthetics monitors endpoints — none of them inject faults.

q: A mission-critical database workload needs 100,000 sustained IOPS from a single EBS volume with sub-millisecond latency. Which EBS volume type meets this requirement?
options: gp3 with provisioned IOPS
st1 throughput-optimized HDD
io2 Block Express, which supports up to 256,000 IOPS per volume with sub-millisecond latency
sc1 cold HDD
explain: io2 Block Express delivers up to 256,000 IOPS per volume at sub-millisecond latency, the only EBS type rated for six-figure IOPS on one volume. gp3 caps at 16,000 IOPS, and st1/sc1 are throughput HDDs unsuitable for high-IOPS transactional workloads.

q: A machine learning team trains models on GPU instances and needs a shared POSIX file system delivering hundreds of GB/s of throughput, with training data staged from S3. Which storage service is purpose-built for this?
options: Amazon FSx for Lustre, a high-performance parallel file system with native S3 integration for ML and HPC workloads
Amazon EFS Standard
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon S3 accessed via the console
explain: FSx for Lustre provides a parallel file system with sub-millisecond latencies and hundreds of GB/s throughput, plus native S3 linking so datasets stage directly from object storage. EFS tops out far below Lustre throughput for this pattern, FSx for Windows serves SMB workloads, and S3 isn't a POSIX file system.

q: An engineering simulation needs 32 tightly coupled nodes with MPI communication requiring low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnects and OS-bypass capabilities. Which EC2 networking feature should the cluster use?
options: Standard ENA networking across multiple AZs
Placement groups in partition strategy
Public IPs with enhanced routing
Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA), which provides OS-bypass, low-latency interconnects for tightly coupled HPC and ML workloads
explain: EFA provides OS-bypass networking with the low latency and high bandwidth MPI workloads need, outperforming standard ENA for tightly coupled communication. ENA lacks OS-bypass, partition placement groups isolate failure domains rather than optimizing interconnects, and public IPs add latency instead of removing it.

q: An application must upload 20 GB files to S3 over unreliable client networks, and failed uploads currently restart from zero. Which S3 mechanism enables parallel, resumable uploads of large objects?
options: S3 Transfer Acceleration alone
S3 multipart upload, which splits objects into independently uploaded parts that can be retried in parallel and resumed
S3 Versioning on the destination bucket
Pre-signed URLs with 7-day expiration
explain: Multipart upload splits large objects into parts uploaded in parallel, so only failed parts retry instead of restarting a 20 GB transfer. Transfer Acceleration speeds transfers but doesn't add resumability, versioning manages object versions, and pre-signed URL expiration controls access duration rather than upload reliability.

q: A CloudFront distribution needs lightweight HTTP header normalization and URL rewrites at the edge with minimal latency overhead. Which edge compute option is designed for these simple, high-volume manipulations?
options: CloudFront Functions, built for lightweight edge logic like header and URL manipulation with sub-millisecond startup
Lambda@Edge with 10 GB memory functions
Origin request policies only
EC2 instances behind the origin ALB
explain: CloudFront Functions run sub-millisecond JavaScript at edge locations specifically for lightweight tasks like header normalization and URL rewrites. Lambda@Edge suits heavier compute with higher overhead, origin request policies only forward headers without transforming them, and EC2 at the origin adds round-trip latency.

q: A public API backed by Lambda is abused by a few clients sending thousands of requests per second, driving up Lambda and downstream database costs. The team wants to serve repeated identical GET responses from cache instead of invoking Lambda. Which API Gateway feature addresses this?
options: API Gateway request validation
Increasing Lambda reserved concurrency
Enabling VPC endpoints for API Gateway
API Gateway caching, which stores responses at the edge of API Gateway with a configurable TTL to absorb repeated requests
explain: API Gateway caching serves repeated GETs from cache for the TTL duration, shielding Lambda and the database from abusive repeat traffic. Request validation checks payload shape rather than absorbing load, reserved concurrency caps rather than caches, and VPC endpoints change network path rather than caching.

q: A leaderboard workload has highly variable cache demand — quiet overnight, then massive spikes during tournaments — and the team is tired of manually resizing ElastiCache clusters. Which caching option scales capacity automatically?
options: ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode disabled
ElastiCache Serverless, which automatically scales cache capacity up and down with demand
A self-managed Redis fleet on EC2
DynamoDB provisioned capacity
explain: ElastiCache Serverless automatically scales cache compute and storage with actual demand, eliminating manual cluster resizing for spiky workloads. Fixed-node ElastiCache requires manual scaling, self-managed Redis adds operational burden, and DynamoDB is a database rather than a managed cache tier.

q: An Aurora cluster serves transactional readers and heavy analytics readers on the same replicas, and analytics queries periodically starve transactional traffic. The team wants read capacity to scale automatically with analytics load. Which feature adds read replicas on demand?
options: Aurora Backtrack
Aurora Global Database
Aurora Auto Scaling for read replicas, which adds or removes replicas based on CPU or connection metrics
Enabling Multi-AZ on the writer
explain: Aurora Auto Scaling adds read replicas when CPU or connection thresholds are breached and removes them when load drops, isolating analytics bursts from transactional readers. Backtrack rewinds data, Global Database spans Regions rather than scaling reads, and Multi-AZ provides failover rather than read scaling.

q: A log analytics platform on Amazon OpenSearch keeps 90 days of logs searchable, but only the last 7 days are queried frequently. The team wants to cut storage costs without losing searchability of older logs. Which OpenSearch storage tiering fits?
options: Keeping all data on hot data nodes
Deleting indexes older than 7 days
Snapshotting to S3 without restore capability
UltraWarm and cold storage tiers, which keep older indexes searchable at far lower cost than hot nodes
explain: UltraWarm and cold tiers store older indexes on S3-backed storage that remains fully searchable at a fraction of hot-node cost — ideal for infrequently queried log history. All-hot storage wastes money, deletion destroys the 90-day requirement, and plain S3 snapshots aren't searchable without restore.

q: Athena queries over 5 TB of timestamped JSON logs in S3 are slow because every query scans all partitions. The team wants partition pruning without running MSCK REPAIR or ALTER TABLE after each new delivery. Which Athena feature automates partition management?
options: Athena workgroups
Partition projection, which lets Athena calculate partition locations from the query predicate without a metastore entry for each partition
Converting JSON to CSV
Increasing the Athena query timeout
explain: Partition projection computes partition paths from column values at query time, enabling pruning on new data immediately with no metastore maintenance. Workgroups manage query isolation and limits, CSV conversion worsens scan efficiency, and longer timeouts don't reduce scanned data.

q: A Kinesis data stream ingests clickstream data with unpredictable viral spikes. Provisioned shards either throttle during spikes or sit idle and waste money the rest of the time. Which capacity mode removes manual shard management?
options: Kinesis on-demand mode, which automatically scales stream capacity with throughput and bills per GB ingested
Doubling the provisioned shard count permanently
Kinesis Data Firehose with a fixed buffer interval
Writing directly to S3 instead of Kinesis
explain: On-demand mode automatically scales throughput capacity up and down with actual traffic, eliminating both throttling during viral spikes and idle-shard waste. Doubling shards permanently overpays during quiet periods, Firehose is a delivery service rather than a stream, and S3 writes lose real-time stream processing.

q: An MSK cluster must sustain higher per-broker throughput for a growing event backbone, and the team wants fewer, more powerful brokers rather than managing many small ones. Which MSK broker type delivers up to 3x more throughput per broker?
options: Standard kafka.m5.large brokers
ZooKeeper-based metadata nodes
MSK Express brokers, which provide higher throughput per broker with simplified scaling
MSK Serverless with provisioned storage
explain: MSK Express brokers deliver up to 3x the throughput per broker of standard brokers, letting the team scale with fewer nodes. Standard m5 brokers cap out lower per node, ZooKeeper nodes handle metadata rather than data throughput, and MSK Serverless scales automatically rather than offering bigger brokers.

q: A database volume needs 8,000 sustained IOPS on a 500 GB volume, but the team doesn't want to pay for a 2.6 TB gp2 volume just to get the IOPS. Which EBS type decouples provisioned IOPS from volume size most cost-effectively?
options: gp2, scaling size to reach the IOPS
io1 with maximum ratio IOPS
Throughput-optimized st1
gp3, which provides a 3,000 IOPS baseline and allows independently provisioning up to 16,000 IOPS regardless of volume size
explain: gp3 lets you provision up to 16,000 IOPS independent of volume size from a 3,000 IOPS baseline, so a 500 GB volume can get 8,000 IOPS without oversizing. gp2 ties IOPS to size (3 per GB), io1 is pricier per IOPS, and st1 is a throughput HDD unsuited to IOPS workloads.

q: A fleet of application servers holds thousands of persistent connections to RDS, and connection storms during deployments overwhelm the database. The team wants connection multiplexing without changing application code. Which approach maintains performance during connection churn?
options: Increasing the RDS max_connections parameter indefinitely
Amazon RDS Proxy, which pools and multiplexes application connections so database connections stay stable during app-level churn
Adding more read replicas
Switching the application to use IAM database authentication
explain: RDS Proxy pools thousands of app connections into a small set of database connections, absorbing deployment connection storms without code changes. Raising max_connections risks database memory exhaustion, read replicas don't reduce connection overhead on the writer, and IAM auth changes authentication rather than connection handling.

q: A Redshift cluster runs nightly ETL jobs and daytime analyst dashboards. The ETL window needs strong isolation so a runaway transform can't starve dashboard queries, but both share one cluster. Which Redshift feature isolates the workloads?
options: Redshift data sharing, which lets the ETL cluster share live data with a separate analytics cluster with isolated compute
Increasing the node count permanently
Disabling concurrency scaling
Moving dashboards to Athena
explain: Data sharing lets a dedicated ETL cluster share live data with a separate dashboard cluster, giving each workload isolated compute over the same data. More nodes on one cluster still share resources, disabling concurrency scaling reduces burst capacity, and moving dashboards to Athena changes the query engine entirely.

q: A fraud-detection graph on Amazon Neptune is read-heavy with global analysts, and the single writer-region cluster adds latency for distant readers. How can the team scale graph reads across Regions?
options: Enabling Neptune Streams only
Vertical scaling of the writer instance
Neptune read replicas (up to 15), including cross-region replicas that offload read traffic near analysts
Migrating the graph to DynamoDB
